items.title: Portcullis
items.text:
Self-hosted YubiKey authentication gateway for your entire homelab.

Portcullis puts a unified authentication layer in front of all your self-hosted applications. Tap your YubiKey to log in -- one identity, one set of credentials, every app.

items.title: Key Features
items.text:
• WebAuthn (FIDO2) -- Passwordless browser authentication with YubiKey tap
  • mTLS (PIV certificates) -- Client certificate auth for APIs, CLI tools, and service-to-service communication
  • 22+ app templates -- Enable apps like Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Grafana, Immich, and more with one click
  • Hub UI -- Web dashboard to manage apps, view logs, configure settings, and control access
  • Per-app access control -- LLDAP groups determine who can access which apps
  • Single sign-on -- Keycloak-powered OIDC/SAML for apps with native SSO support
  • Forward auth -- Transparent authentication for apps without SSO via oauth2-proxy + group-gate
  • Wildcard TLS -- One wildcard certificate covers all subdomains, with automatic renewal via ACME DNS-01
  • Privacy by design -- Individual subdomain names never appear in Certificate Transparency logs
  • Fully self-hosted -- No external auth providers, no cloud dependencies

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
Traefik sits at the edge as a reverse proxy, terminating TLS and optionally requesting client certificates. Behind it, oauth2-proxy and group-gate enforce authentication and per-app access. Keycloak acts as the identity provider, federating users from LLDAP (a lightweight LDAP directory). Vault PKI issues client certificates (30 days, self-service renewal) for mTLS, and revocation is checked on every request.

Apps choose their auth method: forward-auth for apps without SSO support, native OIDC for apps that speak OpenID Connect, header-auth for apps that trust upstream identity headers, or public for apps that need no authentication.

items.title: Architecture
items.text: Portcullis is a collection of services that work together to provide unified authentication for self-hosted applications. This page describes how the components connect and how authentication flows work.

items.title: Component Roles
items.text: Component Role Traefik Reverse proxy. Terminates TLS (one ACME wildcard cert), routes requests by subdomain, applies middleware chains, optionally requests client certificates. Reads Docker labels through its read-only socket proxy. oauth2-proxy Forward authentication. Redirects unauthenticated users to Keycloak (with per-request acr_values for step-up), and returns identity headers and the access token on success. group-gate Per-request authorization (forward-auth). Checks client-cert revocation, the app's auth policy (acr/amr, mTLS binding), the subdomain's required group and path_groups. Returns 403 or a step-up page. Keycloak Identity provider. WebAuthn (FIDO2), X.509 (YubiKey PIV) login with CRL checks, password, Level-of-Authentication step-up, OIDC/SAML for apps. Federates users from LLDAP. LLDAP Lightweight LDAP directory. Stores users and groups (custom user fields are LLDAP attributes). They are managed in the Hub; directory.<domain> redirects to people.<domain> (LLDAP's own UI has no SSO and is reachable only from the server: portcullis lldap-ui). PostgreSQL Database backend for Keycloak. Vault PKI Private CA in server mode (raft, auto-unseal). Issues client certificates (default 30 days) for YubiKey PIV slots and publishes the CRL. Enrollment UI enroll.<domain>: admins enroll WebAuthn and PIV certificates; any user renews their own certificate at /self. Signs CSRs through a least-privilege Vault AppRole. Hub Two listeners: hub.<domain> (admins only): app catalog, runs each enabled template as its own compose project, registers Keycloak clients, writes the policy file and user-attributes.json, reports drift. people.<domain> (any signed-in user): Users & Groups (People, Groups, Org chart, Import), with per-request permission checks (admins, or delegated edit_details / invite / remove permissions). Monitoring (optional) Compose profile monitoring: Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana at metrics.<domain> (lldap_admin), blackbox and textfile exporters. See Monitoring. Socket proxies socket-proxy-traefik (read-only) and socket-proxy-hub (what compose needs): the only containers that mount the Docker socket. See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Repository Structure
items.text:
Portcullis is organized as four separate repositories, each with a distinct responsibility. Their interfaces are defined in Integration Contracts.

  • Core repo (porelli/portcullis) -- docker-compose.yml for all core services, the ./portcullis admin CLI (libraries in scripts/lib/), group-gate (group-gate/), the enrollment UI (enroll/), Traefik dynamic configuration (traefik/), Vault configuration (vault/) and the Keycloak realm export. This is the only repo you need to clone to deploy Portcullis.

  • Hub repo (porelli/portcullis-hub) -- The management web UI, published as a signed container image at ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub (selected with HUB_IMAGE).

  • Templates repo (porelli/portcullis-templates) -- The app templates (<app-id>/manifest.yaml + compose.yml), the manifest JSON Schema and the template validator. The Hub clones it on first startup as the default template source. Accepts outside contributions.

  • Docs repo (porelli/portcullis-docs) -- This documentation site, built with Zensical. App catalog pages are generated from the template manifests.

items.title: Authentication Flows
items.text: Portcullis supports four authentication methods. Each app declares its method in its manifest.yaml.

items.title: Forward Auth (oauth2-proxy + group-gate)
items.text:
Used by apps that have no native SSO support (Pi-hole, DokuWiki, Scrutiny, etc.). Traefik delegates authentication to oauth2-proxy and authorization to group-gate before the request reaches the app. The router's middleware chain is client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file; client-headers@file must come first so group-gate sees the client certificate (for revocation and the mTLS binding).

If the session does not satisfy the app's access policy, group-gate answers with a 403 step-up page that redirects to https://auth.<domain>/oauth2/start?acr_values=<needed>&prompt=login&rd=https://<app>/, and Keycloak prompts for the missing factor. (oauth2-proxy only serves /oauth2/* on auth.<domain>: a host-less router would get Traefik's default TLS options and be refused with 421 on every app host.)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant O as oauth2-proxy
    participant G as group-gate
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant A as App

    U->>T: GET https://pihole.example.com
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 401 (no session)
    T-->>U: 302 Redirect to oauth2-proxy /sign_in
    U->>O: Follow redirect
    O-->>U: 302 Redirect to Keycloak
    U->>K: Keycloak login (WebAuthn / YubiKey tap)
    K-->>U: 302 Redirect to oauth2-proxy /callback
    U->>O: Callback with auth code
    O->>K: Exchange code for tokens
    K-->>O: ID token + access token (includes groups)
    O-->>U: Set session cookie, redirect to app
    U->>T: GET https://pihole.example.com (with cookie)
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 200 OK (X-Auth-Request-*, access token)
    T->>G: Check (host, groups, access token, URI, client cert info)
    Note over G: revocation, policy (acr/amr), group users_pihole, path_groups
    G-->>T: 200 OK (X-Forwarded-User, X-Auth-Request-Groups)
    T->>A: Forward request
    A-->>U: App response

items.title: Native OIDC
items.text:
Used by apps with built-in OpenID Connect support (Jellyfin, Immich, Vaultwarden, Nextcloud, etc.). The app redirects to Keycloak directly, without oauth2-proxy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant A as App
    participant K as Keycloak

    U->>T: GET https://photos.example.com
    T->>A: Forward request
    A-->>U: 302 Redirect to Keycloak authorize endpoint
    U->>K: Keycloak login (WebAuthn / YubiKey tap)
    K-->>U: 302 Redirect to app callback
    U->>T: GET https://photos.example.com/callback?code=...
    T->>A: Forward request
    A->>K: Exchange code for tokens
    K-->>A: ID token + access token
    A-->>U: Set session, app response

items.title: Header Auth
items.text:
Used by apps that accept a trusted identity header from the reverse proxy (Grafana, Kanboard, Firefly III, Guacamole, CloudBeaver). The user authenticates via forward auth, and the app reads X-Forwarded-User (the LLDAP username, set by group-gate; the email travels separately in X-Forwarded-Email). The app accepts that header only from Traefik's fixed IP, so other containers on portcullis-proxy cannot impersonate users.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant O as oauth2-proxy
    participant G as group-gate
    participant A as App

    U->>T: GET https://grafana.example.com
    Note over T,O: Forward auth (same as above)
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 200 OK
    T->>G: Group check
    G-->>T: 200 OK (X-Forwarded-User: alice)
    T->>A: Request from PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP with X-Forwarded-User
    A-->>U: App logs in alice automatically

items.title: mTLS (Client Certificate)
items.text:
When mTLS is enabled, the browser presents the X.509 certificate stored in the YubiKey's PIV slot during the TLS handshake. Traefik verifies it against the Portcullis CA chain, but does not check revocation; that happens in group-gate and Keycloak.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User + YubiKey
    participant T as Traefik
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant G as group-gate
    participant A as App

    U->>T: TLS handshake (client cert)
    T->>T: Verify chain against certs/ca-chain.crt
    U->>T: GET https://auth.example.com/... (login)
    T->>K: via portcullis-auth, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert (PEM)
    Note over K: trusts the header only from Traefik's IP,<br/>re-validates chain + EKU, checks Vault CRL (fail closed)
    K-->>U: Session with amr=mtls (LoA 3)
    U->>T: GET https://app.example.com (cookie + client cert)
    T->>G: forward-auth with X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info
    Note over G: serial not revoked? policy needs mtls only?<br/>then cert CN must equal preferred_username
    G-->>T: 200 OK
    T->>A: Forward request

Routers on the protected tier without forward-auth (e.g. the Vault UI template) rely on the TLS handshake alone: there the certificate works until it expires. See TLS & mTLS.

items.title: TLS Tiers
items.text:
Traefik is configured with three TLS option sets. Each app chooses its tier based on its security requirements.

Tier Traefik TLS Option Client Cert Behavior Use Case protected RequireAndVerifyClientCert Required -- TLS handshake fails without a valid cert Highest security apps (Vault UI) authaware VerifyClientCertIfGiven Optional -- verified if present, WebAuthn fallback if not Most apps (default for forward-auth and OIDC apps) public NoClientCert Not requested Public-facing apps, apps that manage their own auth

When MTLS_ENABLED=false in .env, all three tiers behave like public -- no client certificates are requested for any app. Routers that relied on protected alone become unauthenticated.

For apps the Hub sets the tier from the app's access policy, not from the template (see Authentication Policies).

items.title: Network Topology
items.text:
Traefik is the only service exposed to the internet (ports 80 and 443). It is attached to every network it has to reach; nothing else bridges them.

  • portcullis -- Core services: Keycloak, LLDAP, Vault, PostgreSQL, oauth2-proxy, group-gate, Hub, enroll. Apps are not on it and cannot reach these services directly.
  • portcullis-proxy -- Traefik and app frontend services; Traefik's docker provider routes over it. Fixed subnet (PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET, default 172.31.250.0/24), Traefik always at PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP (default 172.31.250.2), other containers from PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE (which excludes Traefik's IP). Header-auth apps trust identity headers only from Traefik's address.
  • portcullis-auth -- Internal network with only Traefik (fixed PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP, default 172.31.251.2) and Keycloak. Keycloak accepts proxy headers -- including the forwarded client certificate for X.509 login -- only from that address.
  • socket-proxy-traefik, socket-proxy-hub -- Internal networks, each shared by one client and its Docker socket proxy.
  • Per-app networks -- Each app's compose project (portcullis-<app-id>) has its own default network. Internal services (databases, caches, workers) live only there, isolated from all other apps.

Frontend services join both default and portcullis-proxy; internal services only default.

Security & Hardening lists every network's members and addressing rules.

Native OIDC apps that need to reach Keycloak do so over HTTPS via the public URL (https://auth.<domain>), not via the internal network.

DNS is configured as a wildcard record (*.portcullis.example.com), so all subdomains resolve to the same server IP. Traefik routes each subdomain to the correct container based on Docker labels.

items.title: Custom Attributes Flow
items.text:
Custom user fields (department, office, manager, etc.) defined in the Hub flow to apps in two ways:

flowchart LR
    LLDAP[(LLDAP<br/>custom attributes)]
    Hub[Hub<br/>evaluates rules,<br/>reads attributes]
    UAFile[user-attributes.json<br/>hub_data volume]
    GG[group-gate]
    App1[Forward-auth /<br/>Header-auth Apps]
    KC[Keycloak<br/>LDAP mappers]
    Scope[portcullis-attributes<br/>client scope]
    App2[Native OIDC Apps]

    LLDAP -->|GraphQL| Hub
    Hub -->|writes atomically| UAFile
    Hub -->|creates mappers| KC
    UAFile -->|reads on every request| GG
    GG -->|X-Forwarded-Attr-*<br/>percent-encoded, ', ' joined| App1
    KC -->|LDAP sync| LLDAP
    KC -->|attr_<field> claims| Scope
    Scope -->|in ID token| App2

items.title: For Forward-Auth and Header-Auth Apps
items.text:
1. LLDAP: stores users and custom attributes (created by the Hub as non-user-editable LLDAP user attributes).
  2. Hub: reads field values via GraphQL, evaluates rules, writes user-attributes.json (only fields with share_with_apps: true) atomically with the policy file.
  3. group-gate: reads user-attributes.json on every request. On allow, returns X-Forwarded-Attr-<Header-Name> headers. Values are percent-encoded (% → %25, , → %2C), joined with ,, limited to 1 KB per value (before encoding).
  4. Traefik: forwards these headers to the app (the portcullis-groups middleware uses authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr-). Client copies are stripped by the forwardAuth regex.
  5. App: receives the headers. Apps must percent-decode each value after splitting on ,.

items.title: For Native OIDC Apps
items.text:
1. LLDAP: stores users and custom attributes.
  2. Hub: on every field change (create, update, delete, or share_with_apps toggle), syncs Keycloak LDAP attribute mappers on the portcullis-attributes client scope via the Keycloak admin API. Each shared field gets:
    • an LDAP attribute mapper: portcullis-attr-<field> (reads <field> from LDAP)
    • a protocol mapper: attr_<field> claim (user attribute <field> → claim attr_<field> in ID token, access token, userinfo)
  3. Keycloak: syncs users from LLDAP via LDAP federation (periodic and manual sync). The mappers read field values from LDAP.
  4. App: receives attr_<field> claims in the ID token (no percent-encoding; multi-valued fields are JSON arrays).

The Hub attaches the portcullis-attributes client scope as a default scope to every client it creates. On reconcile, it re-attaches missing mappers.

items.title: Expiry Flow
items.text:
Temporary group memberships (manual memberships with expiry, or exceptions with expiry in rule-based groups) are enforced strictly, even while the Hub is down.

flowchart TD
    Admin[Admin sets expiry<br/>or creates exception<br/>with expiry]
    Hub[Hub writes entry<br/>to policy file<br/>expiring array]
    LLDAP[(LLDAP<br/>membership<br/>still present)]
    Eval[Hub evaluator<br/>runs ≤ 60s]
    Check{now >= at?}
    GG[group-gate<br/>reads policy file<br/>on every request]
    Remove[Hub removes<br/>from LLDAP,<br/>revokes Keycloak<br/>sessions]
    Grace[Hub keeps entry<br/>+ 10 min grace]
    Clear[Hub clears<br/>grace entry]

    Admin --> Hub
    Hub -->|immediately| LLDAP
    Hub -->|immediately| GG
    Eval --> Check
    Check -->|not yet| GG
    Check -->|yes| Remove
    Remove --> Grace
    Grace -->|on regrant| Clear
    GG -->|treats as absent<br/>withholds token| App[App denied]
    Remove -->|oauth2-proxy refresh 1m| App2[OIDC apps lose<br/>access within ~1 min]
  1. Admin sets an expiry (date/time) on a membership or exception in the Hub.
  2. Hub writes the entry to the policy file's expiring array immediately: {"user": "<username>", "group": "<group>", "at": "<RFC 3339 UTC timestamp>"}. The entry stays in LLDAP.
  3. group-gate reads the policy file on every request. When now >= at, it treats the membership as absent, regardless of what the user's token says. It also withholds Authorization and X-Forwarded-Access-Token for that request.
  4. Forward-auth apps: denied immediately (403 from group-gate).
  5. Native OIDC apps: the token still has the group claim until the next Keycloak token refresh.
  6. Hub evaluator runs at least every 60 seconds and on changes. When it finds an expired entry, it:
    • removes the membership from LLDAP,
    • revokes the user's Keycloak sessions (so OIDC apps lose access at their next token refresh; oauth2-proxy cookie refresh is 1 minute, so this happens within ~1 minute),
    • keeps the expiring entry (plus a 10-minute grace period) until the membership is actually removed and the grace ends, or until regrant (admin re-adds, exception include, rule change adds them back).

The grace period ensures enforcement stays strict even if the Hub is restarted or LLDAP removal fails: group-gate keeps denying based on the policy file until the Hub successfully removes the entry and clears it.

Property Value Method header-auth SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_cloudbeaver Admin Group admin_cloudbeaver Subdomain db

Auth Notes

Access gated by forward-auth + group-gate. CloudBeaver's reverseProxy auth provider logs users in from X-Forwarded-User (the immutable LLDAP username; the provider has no email header) and trusts team/role headers from any peer with no allowlist, so CloudBeaver is kept off portcullis-proxy behind a small nginx gate (cloudbeaver-gate) that rejects (403) X-Forwarded-User or X-Forwarded-Email from anything but Traefik (PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP) and strips the X-User/X-Team/X-Role/X-Role-TE/name and X-Forwarded-Email headers. Accounts created when the header carried the email are named after it; rename them to the LLDAP username in CloudBeaver's admin UI. Roles and connections are managed in CloudBeaver.

Self-hosted personal finance manager with double-entry bookkeeping

Category: finance Tags: finance, accounting, budget, bookkeeping

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method header-auth SSO Partial Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_firefly Admin Group admin_firefly Subdomain finance

Auth Notes

Uses remote_user_guard: the account is keyed on X-Forwarded-User, the immutable LLDAP username (stored in Firefly's email column; Firefly does not require an address there). X-Forwarded-Email (user-editable in LLDAP) only sets the notification address and never selects an account. remote_user_guard has no proxy allowlist, so the container's nginx rejects (403) any request carrying X-Forwarded-User or X-Forwarded-Email that does not come from Traefik (PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP); TRUSTED_PROXIES is likewise limited to Traefik. Auto-creates user on first login. No group-based admin support. Upgrading from a release that keyed users on email: the old accounts are named after the email; rename them to the LLDAP username (users.email column) before users log in again, or they get new empty accounts.

Complete DevOps platform — Git, CI/CD, container registry, issue tracking

items.title: Authentication

Auth Notes

Full OIDC with Keycloak. git-over-HTTPS, the API, the registry and CI runners are not behind forward-auth and work with personal access tokens. The sign-in, sign-up and OIDC paths (/users/...) are behind forward-auth + group-gate, so only members of users_gitlab can log in or have an account auto-created (GitLab CE has no OIDC group restriction; required_groups and admin_groups are Premium/Ultimate only). Existing GitLab sessions survive removal from the group until they expire; block the user in GitLab to cut access immediately. Admin rights are granted in GitLab (root account uses GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD); admin_gitlab is not mapped. Identity: OIDC identities are keyed on preferred_username (uid_field, the immutable LLDAP username) and omniauth_auto_link_user is false, so an email match never attaches an OIDC login to an existing GitLab account (GitLab instead asks for that account's password). The email is not synced from Keycloak after the account is created. Upgrades: the image is pinned; GitLab must be upgraded along its documented upgrade path (required stops between versions), never by jumping straight to the newest release.

Self-hosted Tailscale control server with Headplane admin UI

Category: vpn Tags: vpn, wireguard, mesh, tailscale

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_headscale Admin Group admin_headscale Subdomain vpn-admin, vpn

Auth Notes

Headscale uses OIDC for node registration. Users are keyed on the OIDC subject (iss + sub) and named after preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username); email_verified_required stays true, so the user-editable, unverified LLDAP email is never synced. Write ACL policy users as "@", never by email. Headplane admin UI has its own OIDC client; it keys its users on sub and links them to the Headscale user with the same sub (its email fallback finds nothing because Headscale stores no unverified email). The first Headplane user becomes owner, later ones get the member role. No group-based access restriction — all OIDC users can register nodes. Post-start step for Headplane: create an API key with docker exec portcullis-headscale-headscale-1 headscale apikeys create --expiration 365d, paste it into the "Headscale API key" setting, then restart the app. Renew it before it expires. Upgrades: Headscale is pinned; upgrade one minor release at a time (its database migrations do not support skipping) and pick the Headplane release that supports that Headscale version.

items.text:
Self-hosted photo and video backup with AI-powered search

Category: media Tags: photos, videos, backup, ai, gallery

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_immich Admin Group admin_immich Subdomain photos

Auth Notes

Full OIDC with auto-register and auto-launch; password login is disabled while OIDC is configured. Promote an SSO user to admin with docker exec <immich-server container> immich-admin grant-admin. roleClaim available but not yet mapped to groups. Identity: OAuth users are keyed on the OIDC sub. Immich also links a login to an existing user with the same email and cannot be told not to, while LLDAP emails are user-editable; so on every start a one-shot job (immich-lock-local-users) gives local, unlinked users (such as the initial admin@portcullis.local) a placeholder OAuth id, and Immich then refuses the email link. Do not create local users in the Immich UI (they are only locked at the next restart); let users sign in with SSO instead. A user who unlinks OAuth in their settings is locked out of SSO until an admin clears the placeholder. Public exceptions (Hub, off by default): shared links still work for signed-in users; turning them on only matters when the policy requires a client certificate at the TLS handshake, which it then no longer does for any path of photos. (mTLS stays enforced at login via the Keycloak acr). Upgrades: immich-server and immich-machine-learning are pinned to the same release and must always move together; read the upstream release notes for breaking changes and keep immich-db on the image upstream specifies.

items.text:
Unified LLM proxy — OpenAI-compatible API for 100+ models with auth and rate limits

Category: ai Tags: llm, ai, openai, proxy, api

items.title: Authentication
items.text:

Auth Notes

OIDC login for the admin UI. The OpenAI-compatible API (and the management API the UI calls) has no forward-auth, so it is reachable with the master key or virtual API keys. The admin UI and all interactive login paths (/ui, /sso, /login, /v2/login, /fallback/login, /onboarding) sit behind forward-auth + group-gate: only members of users_litellm can sign in. SSO users default to the read-only internal_user_viewer role; LLDAP groups are mapped to roles (admin_litellm -> proxy_admin, users_litellm -> internal_user), but that mapping needs the Keycloak "groups" claim in the LiteLLM client's tokens; until the client has the groups scope, SSO users get internal_user_viewer and an admin (logged in with the master key) promotes them in the UI. Users created before this change keep their existing role; review them under Internal Users. Identity: SSO users are keyed on preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username). LiteLLM would otherwise attach an SSO login to any existing user with the same email, and LLDAP emails are user-editable, so the template maps the email attribute to a claim that is never sent: SSO users have no email in LiteLLM. Users created before this change that were keyed on their email need their user_id changed to the LLDAP username.

items.title: ☁ Nextcloud
items.text:
Self-hosted productivity platform — files, calendar, contacts, office

Category: productivity Tags: files, calendar, office, collaboration

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method forward-auth SSO No Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_nextcloud Admin Group admin_nextcloud Subdomain cloud

Auth Notes

Access gated by forward-auth + group-gate; Nextcloud then shows its own login (admin account uses NEXTCLOUD_ADMIN_PASSWORD). No OIDC app is installed yet. Desktop/mobile sync clients and WebDAV cannot pass the forward-auth redirect. Nextcloud does not read the Portcullis identity headers (no user_oidc / header login), so the user-editable LLDAP email plays no part in which Nextcloud account is used. Public exceptions (Hub, off for every share until listed): only the listed share links and the static files their page needs bypass the gateway; logins (Basic auth, remember-me cookies) are not honoured there. The PDF viewer page (a PHP route) is not public, so PDFs on a share download instead of opening inline; Markdown renders only in mode all. Share-password brute force then faces the internet, limited by Nextcloud's own brute-force protection (it sees the client IP via TRUSTED_PROXIES = Traefik). Apps installed under /custom_apps that hook the share page are not covered. Upgrades: the image is pinned; Nextcloud only upgrades one major version at a time, so step through every major (e.g. 33 -> 34 -> 35) and never skip one.

items.title: Sign-in
items.text:
The app has its own login. The Hub's per-app Sign-in setting chooses who signs users in (Apps with their own login):

Plex signs users in with plex.tv accounts. Behind Portcullis sign-in only the web app in a browser works; Plex's TV, mobile and desktop apps can't pass forward-auth and need "App's own login only".

items.title: 🔐 Vaultwarden
items.text:
Lightweight Bitwarden-compatible password manager

Category: security Tags: passwords, bitwarden, vault, secrets

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_vaultwarden Admin Group admin_vaultwarden Admin Paths /admin (require admin_vaultwarden in addition to access) Subdomain passwords

Auth Notes

No public exceptions: Bitwarden Send (1.37.4, web vault v2026.7.0) needs the web vault at / with root-level hashed assets and the password-login token endpoint /identity/connect/token (grant_type=send_access), which no narrow path list can express. Native SSO via OpenID Connect. Users still need a master password for vault encryption. The SSO start and callback paths (/identity/connect/authorize, /identity/connect/oidc-signin) sit behind forward-auth + group-gate, so only members of users_vaultwarden can sign in or get an account by SSO (Vaultwarden has no OIDC group restriction); the API, the token exchange and the Bitwarden clients are not gated. Removing a user from users_vaultwarden blocks new SSO logins, not sessions or devices already signed in (deactivate the user in /admin for that). The admin panel (/admin) is also behind forward-auth + group-gate and, through auth.admin_paths, requires admin_vaultwarden on top of users_vaultwarden; Vaultwarden's ADMIN_TOKEN (VAULTWARDEN_ADMIN_TOKEN) is still required, keep it secret. Identity: SSO accounts are keyed on the OIDC subject (issuer + sub); SSO_SIGNUPS_MATCH_EMAIL stays false, so an SSO login is never attached to an existing registered account by email (LLDAP emails are user-editable). The Keycloak client uses email_verified_claim: false (scope email-unverified: email claim, no email_verified), which Vaultwarden accepts with SSO_ALLOW_UNKNOWN_EMAIL_VERIFICATION, so new users sign up with SSO on their first login and then set a master password. SIGNUPS_ALLOWED is false (accounts only via SSO) and INVITATIONS_ALLOWED is false: an email invitation would create a placeholder account that Vaultwarden hands to the first SSO user presenting that email. Organisations can therefore only add users who have already signed in; check the member's name (their LLDAP username) before confirming them, since the email they were found by is user-editable. Don't use the /admin "Invite user" button (it ignores INVITATIONS_ALLOWED and creates such a placeholder). A user whose email collides with an existing account is refused, never merged.

items.title: Adding an App
items.text:
This guide walks through creating a new app template. Templates live in porelli/portcullis-templates, one directory per app at the repo root. The repo accepts outside contributions, including pull requests from forks.

Start with CONTRIBUTING.md

The templates repo's CONTRIBUTING.md is the authoritative checklist: auth method choice, compose and security rules, image pinning, and what CI runs. This page explains the same steps with examples.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
A template is:

<app-id>/
  manifest.yaml   # what the Hub shows and how auth is wired
  compose.yml     # how the app runs behind Traefik
  ...             # optional support files (config templates, setup scripts)
tests/apps/<app-id>.sh   # its CI test

When a user enables the app, the Hub:

  1. generates a per-app .env from the manifest (settings, generate: random secrets, referenced core variables)
  2. copies the directory to <core>/templates/<app-id>/
  3. registers the manifest's Keycloak clients
  4. starts the compose file as its own project, portcullis-<app-id>
  5. publishes the app's subdomains, group, admin paths and policy to group-gate

items.title: Step 1: Pick an app ID and a subdomain
items.text:
The app ID is lowercase and matches ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}$, e.g. uptime-kuma. It is the directory name and the compose project scope. Pick a subdomain no other template routes. Core subdomains (auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, metrics) are off limits. The Hub refuses to enable two apps that route the same subdomain.

git clone https://github.com/porelli/portcullis-templates.git
cd portcullis-templates
mkdir myapp

items.title: Step 2: Choose the auth method
items.text:
The app... auth.method Router middlewares speaks OpenID Connect and can be pointed at Keycloak native-oidc (+ keycloak_clients) no portcullis-auth; the app logs users in itself can create/log in users from a trusted header (X-Forwarded-User) header-auth portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker has its own login (or none) and no SSO forward-auth portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker is protected by client certificates only mtls tls.options: protected@file, no forward-auth uses a vendor account system (e.g. plex.tv) custom (+ auth.native_login if it has its own login) none: the Hub adds Portcullis sign-in through its override is meant to be public public none

Prefer native-oidc when the app supports it well: mobile apps, API tokens and CLI clients keep working. Then check who can log in:

  • The app can restrict OIDC logins to a group. Configure it with access_group (users_<app-id>) and set group_access: true.
  • It cannot. Then any Keycloak realm user could sign in. Put only the interactive login paths behind forward-auth + group-gate, on a higher-priority PathPrefix router. Keep the API on the host-wide router without forward-auth. See gitlab/, litellm/ and vaultwarden/.
  • It has an admin panel on a path (e.g. Vaultwarden's /admin). Route the path through a gated PathPrefix router and list it in auth.admin_paths. group-gate then also requires admin_group there.

Give SSO-created users the least-privileged role the app has.

If the app has share links for people without an account (public file shares, shared dashboards), declare them in auth.public_access instead of adding an ungated router: the Hub generates the public router when an admin turns the exception on. Read the app's routes at the pinned version and keep the list narrow: {token} paths for per-share listing, static-only supporting paths, exact routes with a justification, and the app's login headers, cookies and query parameters in credential_*.

items.title: Step 3: Write manifest.yaml
items.text:
Copy a template with the same auth method and adapt it: grafana/ for header-auth, scrutiny/ for forward-auth, vaultwarden/ for native OIDC. All fields are documented in the Manifest Reference.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../schema/manifest.schema.json
name: My App
description: A brief description of what the app does
icon: "\U0001F4E6"
category: productivity
tags: [example, demo]

auth:
  method: forward-auth
  sso: false
  group_access: true
  group_admin: false
  access_group: users_myapp
  admin_group: admin_myapp
  notes: Access gated by group-gate. No SSO -- uses its own login.

env:
  - key: MYAPP_SECRET
    description: Secret key for My App
    generate: random

keycloak_clients: []
config_files: []

urls:
  - label: My App
    url: "https://myapp.{{DOMAIN}}"

items.title: Step 4: Write compose.yml
items.text: tests/validate.py checks every rule below.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Networks. Services with traefik.enable: "true" use networks: [default, portcullis-proxy]. Databases, caches and sidecars stay on default only. Declare portcullis-proxy as external: true. No other networks.
  • Routers.
    • Use exactly the form rule: Host(`<sub>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}`). The Hub parses it strictly and rejects anything it can't fully resolve (see Hub → Template rules).
    • Set entrypoints: websecure.
    • Set tls.options to authaware@file, public@file or protected@file. The Hub overrides it from the app's access policy.
    • Include security-headers@file in the middlewares.
  • Middleware order for gated routers: client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file. client-headers@file first lets group-gate check client-cert revocation.
  • Volumes declare name: portcullis_<volume>, unique across templates.
  • Files shipped with the template are mounted as ./templates/<app-id>/<file>, never ./<file>. Compose resolves relative paths against the core checkout on the host. From core, only ./certs/ca-bundle.crt:<path>:ro may be mounted.
  • Variables. Core variables (PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN, PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET, PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE, PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP) always use their default form. Every other variable must be declared in the manifest. Required ones (${VAR:?…}) must be env entries with generate: random. Use $$VAR for variables the container shell should expand.
  • No ports: (declare host ports in the manifest), build:, container_name: or env_file:.
  • Images are pinned by version tag and digest (Step 5).

items.title: Forward-auth / header-auth
items.text:
services:
  myapp:
    image: myorg/myapp:1.4.2@sha256:<index digest>
    environment:
      MYAPP_SECRET: ${MYAPP_SECRET:?generated by the Hub}
    volumes:
      - myapp-data:/data
    networks:
      - default
      - portcullis-proxy
    labels:
      traefik.enable: "true"
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.rule: Host(`myapp.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}`)
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.entrypoints: websecure
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.tls.options: authaware@file
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.middlewares: client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file
      traefik.http.services.myapp.loadbalancer.server.port: "8080"

volumes:
  myapp-data:
    name: portcullis_myapp_data

networks:
  portcullis-proxy:
    external: true

A header-auth app must accept X-Forwarded-User only from ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}. See Header Auth Pattern.

items.title: Native OIDC
items.text:
services:
  myapp:
    image: myorg/myapp:1.4.2@sha256:<index digest>
    environment:
      OIDC_ISSUER: https://auth.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}/realms/portcullis
      OIDC_CLIENT_ID: myapp
      OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET: ${MYAPP_OIDC_SECRET:?generated by the Hub}
      SSL_CERT_FILE: /certs/ca-bundle.crt   # trust the internal/staging CA
    volumes:
      - ./certs/ca-bundle.crt:/certs/ca-bundle.crt:ro
    networks:
      - default
      - portcullis-proxy
    labels:
      traefik.enable: "true"
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.rule: Host(`myapp.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}`)
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.entrypoints: websecure
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.tls.options: authaware@file
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.middlewares: security-headers@file
      traefik.http.services.myapp.loadbalancer.server.port: "8080"

networks:
  portcullis-proxy:
    external: true

Then add the client and its secret to the manifest:

env:
  - key: MYAPP_OIDC_SECRET
    description: My App OIDC client secret
    generate: random

keycloak_clients:
  - client_id: myapp
    secret_env: MYAPP_OIDC_SECRET
    redirect_uri: "https://myapp.{{DOMAIN}}/callback"
    name: My App

Gate an admin path of a native-OIDC app with a second router and auth.admin_paths: ["/admin"]:

      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.rule: Host(`myapp.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}`) && PathPrefix(`/admin`)
      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.priority: "100"
      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.entrypoints: websecure
      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.tls.options: authaware@file
      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.middlewares: client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file
      traefik.http.routers.myapp-admin.service: myapp

items.title: Public
items.text: Same as above with tls.options: public@file, only security-headers@file as middleware, and auth.method: public / group_access: false in the manifest.

items.title: Trusting the internal CA
items.text:
Apps that call Keycloak over HTTPS must trust certs/ca-bundle.crt (system CAs, the Portcullis PKI chain, and the LE staging root when ACME_STAGING=true). Mount it read-only and point the runtime at it:

Runtime Setting Node.js NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/certs/ca-bundle.crt Go SSL_CERT_FILE=/certs/ca-bundle.crt Python (requests) REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/certs/ca-bundle.crt Java Import into the JVM truststore Generic SSL_CERT_FILE or CURL_CA_BUNDLE

items.title: Step 5: Pin the images
items.text:
Every image is pinned to an explicit release and its multi-arch index digest:

image: grafana/grafana:13.3.0@sha256:488984b716c0862639f91a698adbe2862677a5a07bad42da5f03f3030883b205

Get the digest with docker buildx imagetools inspect grafana/grafana:13.3.0 (the top-level Digest:). Floating tags (latest, stable, main, 16-alpine, 2, ...) are rejected.

Add your directory to .github/dependabot.yml (the docker-compose directories: list). Dependabot then proposes tag and digest updates weekly; validate.py fails if the directory is missing. Some updates need care:

  • Don't bump database majors (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis). That needs a data migration.
  • Apps with several images move in lockstep.
  • Apps with upstream upgrade paths say so in auth.notes.

items.title: Step 6: Add a test
items.text:
Create tests/apps/<app-id>.sh. At minimum, a static test (copy tests/apps/scrutiny.sh). Boot the container with compose_up when the app starts reliably in CI. Header-auth apps must call assert_traefik_only_trust and assert_spoofed_identity_rejected.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Test: My App (forward-auth + group-gate)
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.."
source tests/lib.sh
TEST_NAME="myapp"
section "My App"

APP_ID=myapp
SUBDOMAIN=myapp

compose_up "$APP_ID"
IP=$(app_container_ip "$APP_ID")
wait_for_url "http://${IP}:8080" 60 "$APP_ID"

# Unauthenticated access must redirect to Keycloak
assert_redirect_to_keycloak "https://${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN}/"

compose_down "$APP_ID"

See Testing & CI for the helpers.

items.title: Step 7: Run the local checks
items.text:
No Docker daemon is needed:

python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r tests/requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python tests/validate.py myapp      # schema + repo rules (cross-template checks still run)
PATH=.venv/bin:$PATH bash tests/compose-config.sh myapp   # docker compose config -q
shellcheck -S warning tests/apps/*.sh ./*/*.sh

validate.py prints one line per problem with a hint, for example:

ERROR myapp/compose.yml: services.web: image tag 'latest' is floating
      hint: pin the exact release, e.g. postgres:16.15-alpine instead of postgres:16-alpine; ...

The integration tests (tests/apps/*.sh against a real Keycloak/LLDAP/Traefik stack) need the core repo, so you normally let CI run them.

items.title: Step 8: Open a pull request
items.text:
Fill in the checklist of the PR template. What CI does:

Workflow When What Lint (lint.yml) Every push and PR, including forks (no secrets) validate.py, docker compose config for every template, shellcheck, actionlint Test Apps (test-apps.yml) Push to main, every PR including forks (no secrets), manual runs Boots core at the ref in .core-ref, then runs tests/apps/<app>.sh for every changed template

Fork PRs get the full integration tests automatically: core is public and cloned without a token, and no job references a secret. Your PR is tested against the core version in the base branch's .core-ref. The workflow deliberately avoids pull_request_target. Details: Testing & CI.

After the merge, the docs site regenerates the App Catalog from your manifest, and Hub users get the template with Sync.

items.title: Trying it on your own instance
items.text:
Before your PR is merged, add your fork as a template source in the Hub (Template Sources), then enable the app. Useful commands on the core host:

docker compose -p portcullis-myapp ps
docker compose -p portcullis-myapp logs -f
docker compose logs group-gate | grep myapp   # DENIED / ALLOW-UNMAPPED / STEPUP lines

items.title: Checklist
items.text:
• [ ] App ID and subdomain are unique; no core subdomain
  • [ ] manifest.yaml passes the schema; auth method fits the app
  • [ ] compose.yml: networks, Host() form, middleware order, security-headers@file, named volumes, no ports:
  • [ ] Secrets are generate: random; no default passwords
  • [ ] Header-auth: identity header trusted only from PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP
  • [ ] Images pinned tag@sha256:…; directory added to .github/dependabot.yml
  • [ ] tests/apps/<app-id>.sh added
  • [ ] python3 tests/validate.py and tests/compose-config.sh pass

items.title: Header Auth Pattern
items.text: This guide shows how to configure apps that support "reverse proxy authentication" or "trusted header authentication" behind Portcullis. These apps read the authenticated user's identity from an HTTP header set by the forward-auth chain (oauth2-proxy + group-gate), rather than handling authentication themselves.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
User (YubiKey) --> Traefik --> oauth2-proxy --> group-gate --> App (trusts only Traefik's IP)
                                   |
                                   v
                               Keycloak

The user authenticates via oauth2-proxy (which redirects to Keycloak). group-gate then checks groups and policy and returns the identity headers, which Traefik adds to the request. The app reads X-Forwarded-User and logs the user in automatically -- no separate login step.

items.title: When to Use Header Auth
items.text:
Use this pattern when:

  • The app supports reverse proxy / trusted header authentication
  • You want automatic user login based on the Portcullis identity
  • The app does not have native OIDC or SAML support, or you prefer the simpler header approach

In the manifest, this is auth.method: header-auth. The templates validator (tests/validate.py) requires such apps to restrict the header to Traefik and rejects trust-everything values.

items.title: Step 1: Deploy the App
items.text:
Create a compose.yml with the forward-auth middleware chain:

services:
  myapp:
    image: myapp/myapp:latest
    environment:
      # Enable reverse proxy authentication (app-specific setting)
      AUTH_PROXY_ENABLED: "true"
      AUTH_PROXY_HEADER: "X-Forwarded-User"
      # Accept the header ONLY from Traefik (app-specific setting)
      AUTH_PROXY_TRUSTED_IPS: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}
    networks:
      - default
      - portcullis-proxy
    labels:
      traefik.enable: "true"
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.rule: Host(`myapp.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN:-portcullis.local}`)
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.entrypoints: websecure
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.tls.options: authaware@file
      traefik.http.routers.myapp.middlewares: client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file
      traefik.http.services.myapp.loadbalancer.server.port: "8080"

networks:
  portcullis-proxy:
    external: true

After portcullis-auth@docker (oauth2-proxy) and portcullis-groups@docker (group-gate), the upstream request carries:

Header Content Set by X-Forwarded-User, X-Auth-Request-User The LLDAP username (the token's preferred_username) group-gate X-Forwarded-Email, X-Auth-Request-Email The user's email address, for display only group-gate X-Auth-Request-Groups Comma-separated LLDAP groups group-gate (echoed from oauth2-proxy) X-Auth-Request-Preferred-Username The username oauth2-proxy Authorization, X-Forwarded-Access-Token The Keycloak access token (Bearer …) oauth2-proxy X-Forwarded-Attr-<Header-Name> Custom user field values (e.g., X-Forwarded-Attr-Department, X-Forwarded-Attr-Office-Location), if the field is shared with apps group-gate

Custom attribute headers (X-Forwarded-Attr-*): When admins define custom user fields (department, office, manager, etc.) in the Hub's Setup tab and enable "Share with apps", group-gate returns additional headers with the user's field values. Values are percent-encoded (% → %25, , → %2C), joined with , (comma-space), and limited to 1 KB per value (before encoding; longer values are dropped and logged). Apps must percent-decode each value after splitting on ,. Attribute headers are present only when the request is allowed (after auth factors are satisfied). See Integration Contracts §4.1, §5.

Traefik deletes every one of these from the client's request first and only adds the values the forward-auth services returned. Client copies of X-Forwarded-Attr-* are stripped by authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr- on every forwardAuth middleware (CI's browser test sends spoofed copies and checks they are dropped).

Email is never an identity or linking key

X-Forwarded-User is the immutable LLDAP username. X-Forwarded-Email is the user-editable email: LLDAP lets every user change their own address, including to someone else's. That is why Keycloak's LDAP federation has trustEmail=false (tokens carry email_verified=false) and oauth2-proxy keys sessions on preferred_username.

  • Configure the app to identify users by X-Forwarded-User as a username.
  • Use the email for display or notifications at most.
  • Never let the app create, match or link accounts by email. If a header mapping would let the app match existing accounts by email, leave the email out entirely, as the Grafana template does.

items.title: Step 2: Configure the App
items.text: Each app has its own way of enabling reverse proxy authentication. Here are common examples:

items.title: Grafana
items.text:
Grafana, as in the grafana template (log in by username only):

environment:
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_ENABLED: "true"
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_HEADER_NAME: X-Forwarded-User
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_HEADER_PROPERTY: username
  # No GF_AUTH_PROXY_HEADERS email mapping: Grafana's user sync can match
  # accounts by email, and email is never an identity key.
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_AUTO_SIGN_UP: "true"
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_WHITELIST: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}

items.title: Kanboard
items.text:
As in the kanboard template (environment variables of the official image; Kanboard ignores the header unless REMOTE_ADDR is in TRUSTED_PROXY_NETWORKS):

environment:
  REVERSE_PROXY_AUTH: "true"
  REVERSE_PROXY_USER_HEADER: HTTP_X_FORWARDED_USER
  REVERSE_PROXY_DEFAULT_ADMIN: admin
  TRUSTED_PROXY_NETWORKS: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}/32

items.title: Gitea / Forgejo
items.text:
[service]
ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION = true
ENABLE_REVERSE_PROXY_AUTO_REGISTRATION = true
REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION_USER = X-Forwarded-User
REVERSE_PROXY_AUTHENTICATION_EMAIL = X-Forwarded-Email
REVERSE_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXIES = 172.31.250.2/32

items.title: Wiki.js
items.text:
In the admin panel, go to Authentication and add a Header strategy:

  • Header name: X-Forwarded-User
  • Auto-create users: enabled

items.title: pgAdmin
items.text:
AUTHENTICATION_SOURCES = ['webserver']
WEBSERVER_REMOTE_USER = 'X-Forwarded-User'

items.title: Firefly III
items.text:
Firefly III. remote_user_guard has no proxy allow-list, so the template's nginx additionally rejects the header from any peer other than Traefik (see below):

environment:
  AUTHENTICATION_GUARD: remote_user_guard
  AUTHENTICATION_GUARD_HEADER: HTTP_X_FORWARDED_USER
  AUTHENTICATION_GUARD_EMAIL: HTTP_X_FORWARDED_EMAIL
  TRUSTED_PROXIES: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}

items.title: Step 3: Test the Integration
items.text:
1. Navigate to https://myapp.<your-domain>
  2. You should be redirected to Keycloak (via oauth2-proxy)
  3. Authenticate with your YubiKey
  4. You should be logged into the app automatically as the authenticated user

If the app creates users on first login, the user account will be created with the username from the X-Forwarded-User header.

items.title: Apps Without Header Auth Support
items.text:
Some apps do not support trusted header authentication at all. For these, you have two options:

  1. Use forward-auth for access gating only -- The app has its own login system, but oauth2-proxy + group-gate ensure only authorized users can reach it. Set auth.method: forward-auth and auth.sso: false in the manifest.

  2. Use native OIDC -- If the app supports OpenID Connect, configure it to authenticate directly with Keycloak. See the Architecture page for the flow.

items.title: Header Security
items.text:
Clients on the internet can't spoof X-Forwarded-User. Traefik's forward-auth middleware deletes the header from every incoming request and only re-adds the value oauth2-proxy and group-gate return (see Security & Hardening).

Containers are a different matter. Every app frontend shares the portcullis-proxy network, so any compromised container on it could connect to your app directly and claim to be any user. A header-auth app must therefore accept identity headers only from Traefik.

Core gives Traefik a fixed address for this. The portcullis-proxy network has the subnet PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET (default 172.31.250.0/24), and Traefik always sits at PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP (default 172.31.250.2). Both are in the core .env; the Hub receives them through secrets/hub/core.env and copies them into an app's env when its compose file references them. Always use the default form (validate.py enforces it), so the compose file also resolves outside the Hub:

environment:
  GF_AUTH_PROXY_WHITELIST: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}            # Grafana
  TRUSTED_PROXY_NETWORKS: ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}/32          # Kanboard

If an app has no proxy allowlist (Firefly III, Guacamole, CloudBeaver), block the header in front of it. The built-in templates show three ways to do that:

Pattern Example How App's own web server Firefly III An nginx rule returns 403 when X-Forwarded-User comes from any peer other than Traefik Servlet container Guacamole A Tomcat RewriteValve does the same check Gate container CloudBeaver The app stays off portcullis-proxy. A small nginx *-gate service is the only thing Traefik can reach; it rejects spoofed identity headers and strips extra role/team headers

Never use "trust everything" values such as "**", 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0.

The template test helpers in tests/lib.sh check both sides, and header-auth templates must use both. assert_traefik_only_trust <compose> <SETTING> checks the allowlist statically. assert_spoofed_identity_rejected <url> sends a forged X-Forwarded-User from the CI host (which is never Traefik) and expects a 403.

Also make sure the app doesn't publish its HTTP port on the host: a published port would bypass both Traefik and the allowlist.

items.title: User shows as blank or anonymous
items.text:
• Verify the header name matches what the app expects (some apps want HTTP_X_FORWARDED_USER instead of X-Forwarded-User)
  • X-Forwarded-User carries the username; the email is in X-Forwarded-Email
  • Check that the request really comes from Traefik's IP: the app's allow-list must contain PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP
  • Check oauth2-proxy and group-gate logs (docker compose logs forward-auth group-gate)
  • Confirm the app's reverse proxy auth setting is enabled

items.title: User created but lacks admin privileges
items.text: Header auth typically creates users with the lowest privilege level. Admin must be granted manually in the app (or via LDAP group mapping if the app supports it).

items.title: "403 Forbidden" from group-gate
items.text: The user is authenticated but not in the required LLDAP group for this app. Add the user to the users_<app> group in LLDAP.

items.title: App receives no headers
items.text: Ensure the middleware chain includes portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker in that order. Without group-gate the app gets no X-Forwarded-User, because group-gate is what sets it.

items.title: Integration Contracts
items.text:
Portcullis is split across four repositories that meet at a few well-defined interfaces. This page is the single source of truth for those interfaces. Change it first, then change the repos on both sides.

Repo Role porelli/portcullis (core) Compose stack, ./portcullis CLI, group-gate, enroll, socket proxies porelli/portcullis-hub Hub image (ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub) porelli/portcullis-templates App templates (public; accepts outside contributions) porelli/portcullis-docs This site

items.title: 1. Versions and releases
items.text:
• Tags. Every repo uses semver tags vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change to any contract on this page bumps MAJOR in every repo it affects.
  • Hub image. It is published as X.Y.Z, X.Y, X and sha-<short> for tags, and edge for main. Each release image is signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC) and carries SBOM and provenance attestations. There is no latest tag.
  • Core pins the Hub. On core main the HUB_IMAGE default is ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:edge. A core release must pin a released Hub tag by digest, e.g. ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.4.0@sha256:…; release.yml refuses to publish otherwise (the tag must be a published Hub release that still resolves to that digest). Operators override it in .env and should pin tag + digest in production.
  • Core releases carry a CHANGELOG.md section (Keep a Changelog) and a reproducible tarball with VERSION and its sha256; portcullis version reports the core version and the Hub image in use.
  • Core pins its own images. Every image in core's docker-compose.yml is tag@sha256:…; core CI fails on an unpinned one.
  • Templates pin core. The templates CI tests against the core ref in .core-ref in the templates repo: a tag, or main during development.
  • Templates pin their images. Every template image is tag@sha256:… (enforced by tests/validate.py); Dependabot proposes updates.
  • Templates are versioned by tag. The Hub tracks the source's default branch.
  • Current state. No repository has a release tag yet: HUB_IMAGE defaults to edge and .core-ref is main.

items.title: 2. Core environment variables available to templates
items.text:
When a template's compose.yml references a variable, the Hub copies its value into the app's env from /project/.env. That file is not the core .env: core generates it as secrets/hub/core.env on every ./portcullis up, with only the variables below, PORTAL_DISPLAY_NAME, the HEADSCALE_* / HEADPLANE_* / NETBIRD_* / COTURN_* variables, and any names the operator lists in HUB_SHARED_ENV (core secrets are refused). Templates may rely on:

Variable Meaning PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN Base domain; apps live at <sub>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN} PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET Subnet of the portcullis-proxy network (default 172.31.250.0/24) PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE Dynamic allocation range (default 172.31.250.128/25) PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP Traefik's static IP on portcullis-proxy (default 172.31.250.2). The only peer allowed to send identity headers

Always use the default form, e.g. ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-172.31.250.2}. Any other required variable must be declared in the manifest's env: with generate: random. The Hub writes those into the per-app .env.

items.title: 3. Template layout
items.text:
• Location. One directory per app at the root of a template source repo: <app-id>/manifest.yaml and <app-id>/compose.yml. The <app-id> must match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}$.
  • Manifest schema. Manifests must validate against schema/manifest.schema.json in the templates repo (JSON Schema 2020-12). The Hub enforces the same rules and skips templates that fail.

  • Compose invocation. The Hub runs docker compose -p portcullis-<app-id> -f <template>/compose.yml [-f <data>/overrides/<app-id>.override.yml] [-f <data>/overrides/<app-id>.user.yml] --project-directory <core host path> --env-file <data>/env/<app-id>.env up -d --no-deps (and down --remove-orphans; volumes are never removed). The template's compose.yml is read-only to the Hub. The second file is the Hub's override, regenerated from Settings before every up. The third is the operator's custom override (Hub Expert tab), stored outside the template clone; it is validated against the template and may not set traefik.* or com.docker.compose.* labels, networks, network_mode, pid/ipc/uts, privileged, cap_add, devices, security_opt, bind mounts outside ./templates/<app-id>/ and the bind roots (HUB_OVERRIDE_BIND_ROOTS, default /srv:/mnt:/media), unescaped $ (compose interpolation) in any key or value, or YAML !reset/!override tags (full list in Hub Management). So everything this page derives from a template's labels (routes, subdomains, tiers, middlewares) comes from compose.yml and the Hub's override only.

  • Support files. Files that ship with a template are bind-mounted as ./templates/<app-id>/<file>. Compose resolves relative paths against the core checkout on the host. Before every compose up, the Hub copies the template directory to <core>/templates/<app-id>/; core mounts ./templates read-write into the Hub at /project/templates.

  • Networks. Frontends join the external network portcullis-proxy; internal services join only default. Volumes declare name: portcullis_<name>.
  • Middlewares. Forward-auth and header-auth routers use portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker. Native-OIDC host-wide routers must not, nor may mtls, custom or public routers. For a custom template with auth.native_login the Hub's override sets every router's middlewares label: portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,<the template's own> (Portcullis sign-in, the default) or the template's own without the pair ("own login only", only with allow_without_gateway: true; TLS tier public@file, no groups entry). The template is never edited.
  • Public exceptions. A template may declare share-link paths in auth.public_access (enabled_by_default, default_mode listed|all, token_pattern, credential_headers, credential_cookies, credential_query, static_extensions, service, paths[] with prefix (optionally one whole {token} segment), description, supporting, exact, broad + justification); header-auth templates with it also declare auth.identity_headers. Fields and rules: Manifest reference. The template never ships the public router: the Hub generates it (§5). Router and middleware names starting with portcullis-public- are reserved for the Hub.

items.title: 4. Policy file (Hub → group-gate)
items.text:
The Hub writes group-gate-policy.json atomically (temp file + rename) to the hub_data volume. group-gate mounts that volume read-only and re-reads the file on every request.

{
  "version": 4,
  "default":  {"factors": ["mtls", "webauthn"], "op": "any"},
  "policies": {"<subdomain>": {"factors": ["mtls", "webauthn"], "op": "any|all"}},
  "groups":   {"<subdomain>": "<required LLDAP group>"},
  "path_groups": {
    "<subdomain>": [{"prefix": "/admin", "group": "<LLDAP group>"}]
  },
  "public_paths": {
    "<subdomain>": {
      "paths": [{"path": "/s/{token}", "match": "prefix"}, {"path": "/dist", "match": "static"}],
      "token_pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9-]{1,32}$",
      "static_extensions": ["css", "js", "..."],
      "credential_headers": ["Authorization", "Proxy-Authorization"],
      "credential_cookies": ["nc_token"],
      "credential_query": []
    }
  },
  "expiring": [
    {"user": "jsmith", "group": "contractors", "at": "2027-03-31T23:59:59Z"}
  ]
}
  • factors is a subset of mtls and webauthn; the Hub never writes anything else. There is no password factor (no password sign-in exists): group-gate treats it as an unknown factor and denies (fail closed). The Hub rewrites stored policies naming it on load, never into a weaker one (all: dropped; alternative or alone: any of [mtls, webauthn]). op is any or all, and is ignored when there is at most one factor. An empty factor list means public.
  • Unknown values fail closed. An unknown factor, op or key shape, a file that exists but can't be parsed, or a version newer than group-gate supports (currently 4) makes group-gate deny the request.
  • Version 4 (NEW; the Hub always writes 4) adds the expiring array. group-gate serves only version 4. A group-gate that knows only version 3 denies every request on a version-4 file, so the Hub and core must be upgraded together.
    • expiring: an array of {"user": "<lowercase username>", "group": "<LLDAP group>", "at": "<RFC 3339 UTC timestamp>"} entries for temporary group memberships. group-gate treats the membership as absent once now >= at, regardless of what the user's token says. Usernames are lowercase; timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC (e.g., 2027-03-31T23:59:59Z).
    • The Hub writes at most one entry per (user, group) pair: the earliest at when multiple expiries exist for the same membership.
    • The Hub writes every pending expiry into this array so that expiry enforcement is strict even while the Hub is down. The Hub keeps publishing an expired entry until the membership is actually removed from LLDAP, plus a 10-minute grace period afterwards (cleared on regrant). One exception: the end of an "added" exception of a rule group is not written while the user is a current member, the group's rule matches them and the evaluator keeps them (they stay by rule after the end). Manual expiries and grace entries are always written.
    • Which removals revoke Keycloak sessions. The Hub signs the user out of Keycloak (POST …/users/{id}/logout) after: every membership the evaluator removes (rule, exception or expiry), an admin's member removal, a group deletion (every former member), and a password change; a user deletion removes the Keycloak copy. OIDC apps then lose access at their next token refresh, forward-auth sessions within about a minute (oauth2-proxy cookie refresh). Core runs Keycloak's LDAP federation with cachePolicy: NO_CACHE, so that refresh reads the user's current groups and attributes from LLDAP instead of a cached copy.
    • When group-gate strips an expired membership for a request, it also withholds Authorization and X-Forwarded-Access-Token. The portcullis-groups middleware lists both in authResponseHeaders and echoes them to the backend only when the request is allowed.
  • Keys are subdomains only. group-gate looks everything up by the request's subdomain, so policies, groups and path_groups are keyed by the lowercase subdomains that enabled templates route — never by template ID, which could equal another app's subdomain.
  • Routing must be fully visible. The Hub parses every traefik.http.routers.*.rule label in a template's compose file and only accepts literal Host(\.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN…}`)hosts. It rejects any template withHostRegexp/HostHeader/HostSNI, other domains, variables in the label, routers without a rule, TCP routers, or a rule branch that is not restricted byHost()`. A host the Hub can't see would get no policy and no group (fail open).
  • policies has an entry for each subdomain of an enabled template that has a per-app policy. Templates that inherit the default publish nothing; group-gate falls back to default. An override only names factors the app's auth method can enforce (the Hub refuses others with 400: mtls apps only mtls, custom/public apps without Portcullis sign-in none); every app that runs group-gate can enforce both, so for those the default applies unchanged.
  • One owner per subdomain. The Hub refuses to enable a template that routes a subdomain another enabled template already routes. If a collision still reaches the writer, it publishes the stricter policy (higher LoA, then all over any), merges path groups, keeps the group of the lowest template ID, and logs the collision.
  • groups comes from enabled templates with auth.group_access: true: subdomain maps to auth.access_group. Not for a custom app switched to its own login only (its routers have no group-gate); the fail-closed snapshot records that (native_login_only).
  • Fail closed when a template goes missing. At enable time the Hub stores each app's published config (subdomains, groups, admin paths, policy override) in its state. If an enabled app's template later stops loading, the Hub keeps publishing that last known config and reports it as drift. If there is no stored config, every subdomain the app's running containers route (or a running app project that isn't enabled) gets groups[sub] = "__portcullis_deny__". group-gate matches groups exactly and nobody is in that group, so all requests are denied. Never create an LLDAP group with that name.
  • path_groups comes from enabled templates that declare auth.admin_paths (a list of path prefixes). Each prefix requires auth.admin_group, in addition to the subdomain's group.
    • Matching uses group-gate's normalized X-Forwarded-Uri path: percent-decoded once, // collapsed, dot-segments resolved.
    • It is a prefix match on segment boundaries (/admin matches /admin and /admin/x, not /administrator). The longest matching prefix wins.
  • Core subdomains (auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, people, metrics) are never taken from this file. group-gate-map.conf in core owns them.
    • people is accessible to any signed-in user (§5.1); metrics (Grafana of core's optional monitoring profile) is a core subdomain too. All appear in group-gate, the Hub (policy.CoreSubdomains) and the templates validator.
  • public_paths is, per subdomain, the configuration of core's public guard (§5) for an enabled app whose public router exists:
    • paths: {path, match} patterns. match is prefix (segment boundary), exact or static (files below path: dot-free directories, a file name with one of static_extensions). One whole segment may be {token}, which matches one segment that token_pattern (anchored) accepts. Listed share tokens are published as {token}: tokens are secrets and stay in the Hub's state.yaml; Traefik's rule routes only the listed ones.
    • credential_headers (always including Authorization and Proxy-Authorization), credential_cookies, credential_query: credentials the guard refuses.
    • Any unknown key, malformed pattern or bad regex makes the guard deny. Missing-template snapshots keep publishing the entry (the containers keep their public router).
  • Older files. A policy file without a version key is denied by group-gate (only version 4 is served). A missing file (the Hub has never written one, or the volume is gone) is treated as an empty policy with no groups or path groups.

items.title: 4.1 User attributes file (Hub → group-gate) — NEW
items.text:
The Hub writes user-attributes.json atomically to the same directory as the policy file (hub_data volume). group-gate reads it on every request to populate attribute headers for apps. A missing or corrupt file results in no attribute headers being sent (never a deny).

File format (version 1):

{
  "version": 1,
  "fields": {
    "department": "Department",
    "cost_center": "Cost-Center",
    "office_location": "Office-Location"
  },
  "users": {
    "jsmith": {
      "department": ["Engineering"],
      "cost_center": ["CC-1234"],
      "office_location": ["Milan"]
    },
    "alee": {
      "department": ["HR", "Operations"],
      "office_location": ["Berlin"]
    }
  }
}
  • fields: maps each custom field name to its header name. The header name has each underscore-separated word capitalized (e.g., cost_center → Cost-Center). Only fields with the ShareWithApps flag are included. Field names match ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(_[a-z0-9]+)*$ and are at most 31 characters (no leading, trailing or doubled _), so the underscore-to-hyphen-plus-capitalize mapping is injective (no collisions possible) and always gives a valid header name. group-gate skips (and logs) a field whose name or header name is invalid; the other fields still produce headers. Only an unreadable or malformed file (or two fields on one header) means no attribute headers at all.
  • users: maps each lowercase username to their field values. Each field is an array of strings (even for single-valued fields). Users with no shared field values are omitted.
  • Written atomically with mode 0644, using temp file + rename, at the same time as the policy file.
  • Encoding: Each attribute value is percent-encoded before being joined: % becomes %25 and , becomes %2C. After encoding, values are joined with , (comma-space). Apps must percent-decode each value after splitting on ,. The 1 KB limit per value is measured before percent-encoding; a value over 1 KB (before encoding) is dropped and logged.
  • Security: group-gate returns these headers only on allow (after auth factors are satisfied). Client copies of X-Forwarded-Attr-* headers are stripped by authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr- on every forwardAuth middleware in Traefik (Traefik cannot delete headers by prefix in a headers middleware, so each middleware's regex is the mechanism). Routers without a forwardAuth middleware in their chain (such as keycloak, vault-ui, enroll-invite, headscale, netbird, and docs) do not strip these headers, so backends on those routes must not trust X-Forwarded-Attr-* headers.
  • Logging: A corrupt user-attributes.json file is logged by group-gate; no attribute headers are sent (never a deny).

items.title: 5. Hub ⇄ Traefik
items.text:
• Proxy secret. Traefik adds the header X-Portcullis-Proxy-Secret: ${HUB_PROXY_SECRET} to every request it routes to the Hub, using a headers.customRequestHeaders middleware on the Hub router.
    • The Hub rejects any request without a matching header, compared in constant time.
    • The only exception is GET /healthz.
    • HUB_PROXY_SECRET is generated by portcullis init, and the Hub refuses to start without it.

  • Identity headers. Behind portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker, every backend (the Hub, enroll, header-auth apps) receives:

    • X-Forwarded-User and X-Auth-Request-User: the immutable LLDAP username (preferred_username; oauth2-proxy userIDClaim)
    • X-Forwarded-Email and X-Auth-Request-Email: the user-editable email (LLDAP lets users change it; Keycloak trustEmail=false)
    • X-Auth-Request-Groups: comma-separated groups

    Traefik guarantees these because each one is listed in the forward-auth middlewares' authResponseHeaders, so client copies are deleted. The Hub shows X-Forwarded-User as-is and never looks the signed-in user up in LDAP to identify them. Its LLDAP service account (§9) is used only for user and group management. - Attribute headers (NEW). When custom user fields are defined (§9.6) and the ShareWithApps flag is enabled on a field, group-gate returns additional headers on every request it allows through portcullis-groups: - X-Forwarded-Attr-<Header-Name>, where <Header-Name> is the field's name with each underscore-separated word capitalized (e.g., cost_center → Cost-Center). - Values are percent-encoded (% → %25, , → %2C), then joined with , (comma-space). Control characters (ASCII 0x00–0x1F and 0x7F) are stripped from each value before encoding. Each individual value is limited to 1 KB (measured before percent-encoding); longer values are dropped (not truncated) and logged by group-gate. Apps must percent-decode each value after splitting on ,. - group-gate reads field values from user-attributes.json (§4.1). A missing or corrupt file results in no attribute headers (never a deny). Users absent from the file get no attribute headers. - Scope: attribute headers are returned for all requests that pass through portcullis-groups, including app subdomains and core subdomains (auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, people, metrics). They are not returned on public routers (which have no portcullis-auth or portcullis-groups middlewares). - Forwarding: Client copies of X-Forwarded-Attr-* headers are stripped by authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr- on every forwardAuth middleware. Traefik cannot delete headers by prefix in a headers middleware, so the regex on every forwardAuth middleware is the stripping mechanism. Routers without forwardAuth in their chain (such as keycloak, vault-ui, enroll-invite, headscale, netbird, and docs) do not strip these headers, so backends on those routes must not trust X-Forwarded-Attr-* headers. - Email is never an identity or linking key. No repo may authorise, create, match or link accounts by email. Native-OIDC templates key accounts on sub / preferred_username. - Order. On the Hub router, hub-proxy-secret@docker comes after portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker, so the secret is never sent to oauth2-proxy or group-gate. - TLS tier per host. Traefik selects TLS options per SNI host, so every router of a host must carry the same tls.options; on a mismatch Traefik uses its default options and answers 421 Misdirected Request. The Hub writes one tier for all routers of an app: public@file, authaware@file or protected@file from the app's effective policy (its override or the default, intersected with what its method can enforce: an mtls app always gets protected@file, an app that handles its own sign-in public@file), except that protected@file becomes authaware@file for all of the app's routers while its public router exists (policy.HostTier). - Public router. When an app's public exceptions are on and open at least one path, the Hub's override adds, on the public_access.service (default: the only routed service): - traefik.http.routers.portcullis-public-<app>: rule Host(`<host>`) && (<entries>) over the app's hosts on that service. Entries: Path(`p`) || PathPrefix(`p/`) for prefixes (and each listed {token} expansion), Path(`p`) for exact paths, and for other supporting paths PathRegexp(`^p(/[A-Za-z0-9_~@+-]+)*/[A-Za-z0-9_~@+-][A-Za-z0-9._~@+-]*\.(<static extensions>)$`) (written with compose's $$). Then entrypoints: websecure, the host's tier, a priority above every router of the app (explicit priorities, and rule length plus 253 per ${…} for implicit ones), the service's single Traefik service; - middlewares portcullis-public-guard@docker,portcullis-public-strip-<app>@docker,rate-limit@file,security-headers@file (rate-limit and security-headers come from core's traefik/dynamic/middlewares.yml). No portcullis-auth, no portcullis-groups; - traefik.http.middlewares.portcullis-public-strip-<app>.headers.customrequestheaders.<H>: "" for each core identity header (X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email, X-Forwarded-Groups, X-Forwarded-Preferred-Username, X-Forwarded-Access-Token, X-Auth-Request-User, -Email, -Groups, -Preferred-Username, -Access-Token, Remote-User, -Email, -Groups, -Name), Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, each auth.identity_headers and public_access.credential_headers entry, each also with _ for -. Without forward-auth nothing else deletes client copies; core's entrypoints also drop alias headers (aliasHeadersStrategy=delete). - Public guard (core). portcullis-public-guard@docker is a forwardAuth middleware defined on group-gate (http://group-gate:8080/public-guard, no authResponseHeaders). It runs first, so it sees the request before the strip middleware. It answers 403 (no redirect) unless: - the policy file is version 4 and has a public_paths entry for the request's subdomain (never a core subdomain); - X-Forwarded-Uri has no #, no encoded /, \, NUL or # in the path, and every normalised form of the path (decoded once, // collapsed, dot-segments resolved; as for path_groups) is inside a published pattern; - no request header is a credential header (case-insensitive, _ read as -); - no cookie (every Cookie header, split on ; and ,) and no query key (everything after the first ?, split on & and ;) names a credential. Names are compared case-insensitively after PHP's mangling (php-src main/php_variables.c, php_register_variable_ex: leading spaces dropped, and . become _, name[…] is name, an unclosed [ becomes _, NUL ends the name), both raw and percent- / +-decoded; a name that isn't valid UTF-8 after decoding (overlong forms) or has control characters is refused.

    On allow it returns 200 without identity headers. Its logs mask token-like path segments and show query parameter names only. - Exposure drift. The Hub compares every exposure label of each running container (each router's tls.options, all portcullis-public-<app> router labels and the strip middleware, and every router's middlewares of native_login apps) with what it would render now, PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN expanded; any difference is public_access_mismatch drift.

items.title: 5.1 People subdomain (NEW)
items.text:
