items.text: A policy with no factors means group-gate requires no particular factor, and the Hub sets the router's tier to public@file. The Hub only changes tls.options. The template's middlewares stay as they are, so a forward-auth app still requires a Keycloak login and its group. An app is only reachable without logging in if its routers have no forward-auth middleware (auth.method: public, a custom app, or one switched to its own login only). An mtls app never becomes public: it keeps requiring the certificate.

items.title: Traefik TLS tier
items.text:
The effective policy also drives the TLS tier on each router via a Hub-generated compose override:

Policy Tier Behaviour Public, or the app handles its own sign-in public@file No client cert mTLS-only, or all of [..., mtls] protected@file Requires client cert at TLS handshake Everything else authaware@file Client cert tolerated but not required

The tier change is emitted as a per-router traefik.http.routers.<name>.tls.options label in ${HUB_DATA_DIR}/overrides/<app>.override.yml, for every router of the app. Base compose.yml files in templates are untouched. Changing the global default restarts only the inheriting apps whose tier actually changed.

One tier per host. Traefik selects TLS options per SNI host, before it knows the path, so every router of a host must share one tier. If two routers of a host disagree, Traefik falls back to its default TLS options and answers 421 Misdirected Request. The Hub therefore always writes the same tier for all of an app's routers, including its public router.

items.title: Public exceptions
items.text:
Templates can declare share-link paths in auth.public_access; an admin turns them on per app in the Hub. While on, the Hub adds a router portcullis-public-<app> for those paths only:

  • higher priority than every router of the app, so it wins for its paths;
  • middlewares portcullis-public-strip-<app>@docker,rate-limit@file,security-headers@file only: no forward-auth, no group-gate, so no login, no group, no hardware key, no step-up and no access policy apply on these paths;
  • the strip middleware deletes client-supplied identity headers (core's X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email, X-Forwarded-*, X-Auth-Request-*, Remote-*, plus the template's identity_headers, each also in its _ form), so a header-auth app can't be told who the visitor is;
  • its first middleware, portcullis-public-guard@docker (group-gate /public-guard), re-checks the path against the published patterns and answers 403 to requests carrying Authorization, Proxy-Authorization or the template's credential headers, cookies or query parameters (names normalised the way PHP does), so a stolen password, API key or session can't get past the hardware key there;
  • supporting paths serve static files only (by extension), plus single exact routes the template justifies;
  • in mode listed, only the share tokens an admin listed are routed; any other token on the same prefix still goes through forward-auth.

Exceptions vs mTLS. A policy of mtls alone, or all including mtls, normally gives the host protected@file: no client cert, no TLS handshake. Anonymous visitors can't present one, so while the public router exists the Hub uses authaware@file for all of the app's routers instead (policy.HostTier). What still enforces mTLS:

App type Gated paths after the downgrade forward-auth / header-auth group-gate's mTLS binding requires a valid, unrevoked client certificate matching the user on every request, so mTLS stays enforced per request native-oidc (no group-gate on the host-wide router) mTLS is only enforced at login, through the Keycloak acr (mtls). An existing app session works from a browser without the key any router without group-gate loses the handshake check; the Hub lists such routers in the warning

In mode listed with no listed share there is no public router and no downgrade. Policies that already give authaware@file or public@file are unchanged.

items.title: Where policies are published
items.text:
The Hub writes per-app policies into group-gate-policy.json keyed by every subdomain the app routes (never by template ID); apps that inherit the default publish nothing and group-gate uses the file's default. A policy with an unknown factor or op makes group-gate deny the request (fail closed). Format: Integration Contracts §4.

For native-OIDC apps the policy also sets the Keycloak client's default.acr.values, so Keycloak prompts for the right level at login.

items.title: Identity
items.text: Policies decide how a user signed in; who the user is always comes from the immutable LLDAP username (preferred_username, X-Forwarded-User), never from the email. LLDAP users can edit their own email, so Keycloak does not trust it (trustEmail=false) and nothing in Portcullis authorises or links accounts by it. See Security & Hardening.

items.title: mTLS binding
items.text: amr=mtls in a token only proves a certificate was used at login. When a policy is satisfied only through mtls (mtls alone, all including mtls, or any where mtls is the only factor in the token), group-gate additionally requires the current request to present an unrevoked client certificate whose CN equals the token's preferred_username. Otherwise the user gets the step-up page. A session opened with a since-revoked certificate, or replayed from a browser without the key, stops working at once. See TLS & mTLS.

items.title: Enforcement map
items.text:
Layer Public WebAuthn mTLS AND combinations OR combinations Traefik public authaware protected protected if mtls in set authaware unless mTLS-only Keycloak none LoA 2 flow LoA 3 flow highest LoA + step-up lowest LoA (any satisfies) group-gate no factor check require hwk ∈ amr require mtls ∈ amr + mTLS binding require all factors in amr (+ binding if mtls) require amr ∩ factors ≠ ∅ (+ binding if only mtls matched)

The table is per factor of the effective policy; which layers apply depends on the auth method (above).

items.title: LLDAP passwords
items.text: The browser flow never asks for an LLDAP password. LLDAP passwords remain for LLDAP's own web UI and for apps that bind to LDAP themselves. They are no policy factor.

items.title: Caveats
items.text:
• acr_values is advisory at Keycloak. The OIDC spec treats it as a hint; Keycloak only hard-rejects when a client requests via the claims parameter with essential: true. Portcullis uses the LoA conditional executors instead, which hard-fail when the user can't satisfy the level (e.g. asking for mtls without a certificate). group-gate also verifies acr/amr from the issued token as a belt-and-braces check — trust doesn't depend on Keycloak honoring the request.
  • Session LoA accumulates. Once a user steps up to LoA 3 via mTLS, every subsequent app within the same session sees acr=mtls and amr ⊇ [mtls, ...]. Stricter apps pass without additional prompts. Loosening policies mid-session doesn't downgrade the session.
  • max_age in the LoA conditions is 10 hours (matching the session lifespan). Lower this in realm-export.json if you want the re-prompt window to be shorter.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
"Step up required" page from group-gate Your session is missing the factor(s) the app requires. Click the link in the page body to re-authenticate at the right level.

Client cert prompt loops indefinitely Your browser may not be sending the client certificate. Check that the cert is imported into your OS/keychain and that the origin matches the Traefik wildcard (*.<your-domain>).

Keycloak login form appears when you expected SSO The session cookie expired (8 hours idle / 12 hours max by default). Re-authenticate.

AND policy keeps failing even after a WebAuthn step-up Check that the acr client scope is attached to the app's Keycloak client and that the acr loa level protocol mapper has Add to access token = true. ./portcullis keycloak configure does this for portcullis-forward-auth, and the Hub attaches the acr and groups scopes to every client it registers; a manually-created client may be missing them.

items.title: Backups
items.text:
./portcullis backup makes a consistent backup while everything keeps running. --offsite also uploads it, encrypted, to a restic repository on another machine or in object storage. ./portcullis backup verify proves that a backup can be restored, and ./portcullis restore puts one back, on the same host or on a new one.

A backup is the keys to everything

A backup contains secrets/, which holds the Vault root token and unseal key, plus .env with every password. Whoever has a backup can decrypt the CA and impersonate any user. For off-host copies, that also takes BACKUP_PASSWORD.

  • Local backups are mode 0700.
  • Off-host copies are only as safe as BACKUP_PASSWORD.

Store BACKUP_PASSWORD offline

./portcullis init generates BACKUP_PASSWORD. Keep a copy in a password manager or on paper in a safe, not only in .env. If the host is lost, .env is lost with it, and the off-host backups are useless without the password. Never rotate it: existing snapshots are encrypted with it.

items.title: What is backed up, and how
items.text:
Piece How Why this way Vault (CA keys, issued-cert records, CRL, AppRole) Raft snapshot (sys/storage/raft/snapshot, root token) → vault.snap Consistent point-in-time copy without stopping Vault Keycloak database pg_dump -Fc → postgres.dump A raw copy of a running Postgres data directory is not consistent LLDAP (lldap_data) Files, with every SQLite database copied through SQLite's online backup API → lldap_data.tar.gz Consistent while LLDAP runs. Keeps private_key (password hashing) Hub state (hub_data), ACME account and certs (traefik_acme) Same → hub_data.tar.gz, traefik_acme.tar.gz .env, certs/, secrets/, config/, keycloak/realm-export.json, headscale/config.yaml, docker-compose.override.yml Copied MANIFEST.json Format, time, core version, Hub image, sha256 of every file verify and restore refuse a backup whose files changed

A backup is built in backups/<timestamp>.partial/ and renamed to backups/<timestamp>/ when it is complete. The newest BACKUP_KEEP_LOCAL (default 7) local backups are kept. ./portcullis upgrade makes one first.

App data in Hub-managed apps (their own portcullis_* volumes) is not part of the core backup.

First backup on a fresh host

On a host without the group-gate image (a fresh install before the first portcullis up, or after docker image rm), ./portcullis backup builds it first (needs network access to Docker Hub and PyPI for the pinned, hashed Python dependencies: cryptography, PyJWT).

./portcullis backup            # local backup
./portcullis backup --list     # local backups

items.title: Off-host backups (restic)
items.text:
Configure the repository in .env:

# Any restic backend the container can reach: s3:, b2:, azure:, gs:, rest:,
# or a local path (e.g. an NFS / USB mount).
BACKUP_REPOSITORY=s3:https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/portcullis
# BACKUP_PASSWORD is generated by ./portcullis init: copy it somewhere offline.

# Provider credentials (restic's variable names). BACKUP_<NAME> wins over
# <NAME>, so BACKUP_AWS_* can differ from the AWS_* used for Route53 / ACME.
BACKUP_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
BACKUP_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
# B2_ACCOUNT_ID / B2_ACCOUNT_KEY, AZURE_ACCOUNT_NAME / AZURE_ACCOUNT_KEY,
# GOOGLE_PROJECT_ID, RESTIC_REST_USERNAME / RESTIC_REST_PASSWORD, ...

# Retention applied after every upload (restic forget --prune).
BACKUP_KEEP_DAILY=7
BACKUP_KEEP_WEEKLY=4
BACKUP_KEEP_MONTHLY=6

./portcullis backup --offsite                 # local backup, then upload + retention
./portcullis backup --list --offsite          # restic snapshots
./portcullis backup --list --offsite --json   # restic's JSON

How the upload runs:

  • Container. restic runs in its pinned image (BACKUP_RESTIC_IMAGE in the core repo's scripts/lib/backup.sh) as your user, with a read-only root filesystem and no capabilities.
  • Secrets. The repository password and the provider credentials are passed to the container by variable name, never on a command line.
  • Snapshots. The first upload initialises the repository. Every snapshot has host portcullis, tag portcullis and path /portcullis-backup, so all runs form one deduplicated, incremental series.

sftp: and rclone: repositories are not supported: the container has neither SSH keys nor rclone. Use rest: with rest-server instead.

items.title: Verify
items.text:
./portcullis backup verify                    # off-host: latest snapshot
./portcullis backup verify --snapshot 1a2b3c4d
./portcullis backup verify --local            # newest local backup (or --local DIR)

Off-host verification first runs restic check, reading BACKUP_VERIFY_READ_DATA (default 10%) of the pack data. Then it restores the snapshot into a temporary directory and checks it like a local backup:

  • every file matches MANIFEST.json, and .env, the root token and the unseal key are present
  • vault.snap is a raft snapshot (meta.json, state.bin, its SHA256SUMS)
  • postgres.dump restores into a throwaway Postgres container (no network) and contains the Keycloak realms
  • the LLDAP database opens, passes integrity_check and has users
  • every volume archive is readable

The command exits non-zero if anything fails. Run it regularly, e.g. weekly: a backup that was never restored is a hope, not a backup.

items.title: Schedule (systemd timer)
items.text:
The backup has to drive Docker on the host (docker exec, throwaway containers), so it runs from a systemd timer, not from a container. A scheduler container would need the Docker socket, which only the socket proxies may mount (contract §6).

./portcullis backup schedule --systemd --output /tmp/units
sudo install -m 0644 /tmp/units/portcullis-backup.service /tmp/units/portcullis-backup.timer /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now portcullis-backup.timer
sudo systemctl start portcullis-backup.service    # once now; journalctl -u portcullis-backup

What the service does:

  • What it runs. portcullis backup --offsite (just backup while BACKUP_REPOSITORY is unset), then portcullis status --textfile.
  • When. Daily at 03:15, plus up to 30 minutes of random delay, catching up after downtime. Change it with --on-calendar SPEC.
  • As whom. The user who generated the units. That user must be allowed to run docker.
  • Metrics. Both commands publish metrics for the monitoring profile, which alerts when the last successful local or off-host backup is older than 36 hours.

items.title: Restore
items.text:
./portcullis restore --list                     # local backups
./portcullis restore --list --offsite           # restic snapshots
./portcullis restore backups/20261031-031500    # a local backup
./portcullis restore --from-offsite             # latest off-host snapshot
./portcullis restore --from-offsite 1a2b3c4d    # a specific one

The restore first checks the backup's checksums and saves the current .env, secrets/ and certs/ to backups/pre-restore-<timestamp>/. Then it stops Portcullis and:

  1. Restores .env, certs/ and the config files. An existing config/ repo is left alone.
  2. Recreates the Postgres and Vault volumes, and pg_restores the Keycloak database into the fresh Postgres.
  3. Initialises the fresh Vault with throwaway keys, then force-restores the raft snapshot, which brings back the original keyring. It installs the backed-up secrets/ and recreates Vault, which auto-unseals with the original unseal key.
  4. Restores the LLDAP, Hub and ACME volumes.
  5. Runs vault init, which refreshes the enroll AppRole secret and the metrics token. Then it starts everything and waits for Vault, Postgres, LLDAP and Keycloak.

Use --yes to skip the confirmation.

items.title: On a new host
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/porelli/portcullis.git && cd portcullis
export BACKUP_REPOSITORY=s3:https://...  BACKUP_PASSWORD='<from your offline copy>'
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...   # the provider credentials
./portcullis restore --from-offsite

.env comes from the backup. Then point DNS at the new host. The ACME certificate is restored too, so Traefik doesn't have to re-issue it.

See the CLI Reference for every option.

items.title: CLI Reference
items.text:
Everything an operator does on the Portcullis host goes through one command in the core checkout: ./portcullis. There are no other scripts.

./portcullis help              # list every command
./portcullis <command> --help  # options of one command

--help works without .env or Docker. Argument errors exit with status 2.

Generated from the real help text

This page restates the output of ./portcullis help and ./portcullis <command> --help in the core repo. If the two ever disagree, the CLI is right.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• .env is parsed, never sourced. Variables in your shell environment win over .env, the same way docker compose resolves them.
  • Secrets never go on the command line. DNS credentials are read from the environment or a hidden prompt. The Vault admin token comes from VAULT_TOKEN or from secrets/vault-init.json.
  • Every setup step is idempotent. init, upgrade, vault init, pki setup, keycloak configure and oidc register can be re-run safely.

items.title: Command overview
items.text: Area Command What it does Setup and lifecycle init First-time setup: .env and secrets, Vault, PKI, Keycloak, start up Start or update the core stack and wait until it is healthy down Stop the core stack. Volumes and secrets are kept upgrade Back up, pull, re-run the idempotent setup steps, restart status Health overview (--json for machines, --textfile for Prometheus) version Core version and the Hub image in use Backups backup Consistent backup to backups/ (--offsite: also restic, encrypted) backup verify restic check + restore + sanity checks (or --local) backup schedule systemd timer for daily backups restore Restore a local or off-host (--from-offsite) backup Configuration config apply Apply ACME_STAGING / MTLS_ENABLED, rebuild the CA bundle config init Keep your settings in config/, a separate git repo dns setup Create A/AAAA records for the domain and its wildcard Vault and PKI vault init Initialise and unseal Vault, set up the enroll AppRole vault unseal Unseal Vault and wait until it is active vault rotate-enroll-secret Issue a new enroll AppRole secret-id pki setup Create the client-certificate CA (idempotent) Identity keycloak configure Import or patch the portcullis realm oidc register Create the core OIDC clients and push their secrets from .env invite One-time setup link: register a passkey, signed in (no password) lldap-ui Break-glass SSH tunnel to LLDAP's own web UI (server only) Client certificates (YubiKey PIV) cert enroll New key and certificate on a YubiKey cert renew New certificate for the key already on the YubiKey cert revoke Revoke a certificate (enforced by group-gate) cert list List issued certificates cert sync Rewrite the revoked-serial list from Vault

items.title: init
items.text:
portcullis init [--domain DOMAIN] [--email EMAIL] [--dns-provider NAME]
                [--non-interactive] [--env-only] [--skip-dns] [--no-config-repo]

First-time setup. It creates .env (mode 0600) with every secret randomly generated: the Postgres password, the Keycloak admin password, the LLDAP admin password and JWT secret, the forward-auth client and cookie secrets, and HUB_PROXY_SECRET, and BACKUP_PASSWORD for off-host backups. Then it runs these steps in order:

  1. DNS records (dns setup)
  2. Vault init, unseal and enroll AppRole (vault init)
  3. CA bundle
  4. docker compose up
  5. Vault PKI, including a self-signed wildcard server cert for local use (pki setup --with-server-cert)
  6. Keycloak realm (keycloak configure)
  7. OIDC clients (oidc register)
  8. config/ repo (config init)

If .env already exists it is kept, and only empty or missing secrets are generated. Every step is idempotent, so you can re-run init after a failure.

Option Meaning --domain DOMAIN Base domain (default: $PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN, otherwise a prompt) --email EMAIL Let's Encrypt account email (default: admin@DOMAIN) --dns-provider NAME cloudflare, porkbun, route53, digitalocean, hetzner, none, or another lego provider name (default: cloudflare) --non-interactive Never prompt. DNS credentials must be in the environment (e.g. CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=...) --env-only Only write or complete .env, then stop --skip-dns Do not create DNS records --no-config-repo Do not create the config/ git repo

DNS provider credentials are read from the environment or a hidden prompt, never from the command line. See Quick Start.

items.title: up
items.text:
portcullis up

Starts or updates the core stack. It checks .env and the portcullis-proxy network settings, creates the bind-mount sources, and rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt. Then it runs docker compose up -d --build and waits for vault, postgres, lldap and keycloak to be healthy. Vault unseals itself on start.

items.title: down
items.text:
portcullis down

Stops and removes the core containers (docker compose down). Volumes and secrets/ are kept. Apps enabled in the Hub run as their own compose projects and are not touched.

items.title: upgrade
items.text:
portcullis upgrade [--skip-backup]

Updates a running installation after git pull:

  1. Generates any missing HUB_PROXY_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_*, LLDAP_JWT_SECRET or BACKUP_PASSWORD. Other secrets must already be in .env.
  2. Creates a local backup (portcullis backup: Vault snapshot, pg_dump, volumes, .env, certs/, secrets/).
  3. Pulls images.
  4. Re-runs the idempotent setup steps: vault init, pki setup (client role incl. CLIENT_CERT_TTL, Keycloak truststore) and the CA bundle.
  5. Runs docker compose up -d --build and waits for health.
  6. Runs keycloak configure and oidc register.
Option Meaning --skip-backup Do not create a backup first

See Upgrading.

items.title: status
items.text:
portcullis status [--json | --textfile]

Prints a health overview:

  • compose services
  • Vault: sealed/active, CA expiry, issued certs, and client certs expiring within CERT_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS (default 7) days
  • Keycloak: realm, users, forward-auth client
  • LLDAP and Traefik

Exits 1 if a core service is down or unhealthy, or if Vault is not active. Otherwise it exits 0.

Option Meaning --json Machine-readable output (same exit status). Expiring certs are in vault.certs_expiring --textfile Write the same data as Prometheus metrics to monitoring/textfile/status.prom for the monitoring profile: service health, Vault active, CA and per-user client-cert expiry. Run it after every scheduled backup (the systemd unit does)

items.title: version
items.text:
portcullis version [--json]

Prints the core version and the Hub image in use:

  • Core version. The VERSION file of a release tarball, else git describe of the checkout.
  • Hub image. HUB_IMAGE from .env or the environment, else the default pinned in docker-compose.yml, plus the image of the running Hub container if there is one.
Option Meaning --json Machine-readable output

items.title: Backups
items.text: See Backups for the full picture.

items.title: backup
items.text:
portcullis backup [--offsite] [--list [--json]]

Creates a consistent backup in backups/<timestamp>/ (mode 0700) while everything keeps running. It contains:

  • a Vault raft snapshot
  • a pg_dump of the Keycloak database
  • the LLDAP, Hub and ACME volumes (SQLite via its online backup API)
  • .env, certs/, secrets/, config/ and the config files
  • MANIFEST.json with the sha256 of every file

It keeps the newest BACKUP_KEEP_LOCAL (default 7) local backups.

The backup contains the Vault root token and unseal key

It can decrypt the CA and every secret. Protect it like the keys.

Option Meaning --offsite Also upload it to the restic repository BACKUP_REPOSITORY, encrypted with BACKUP_PASSWORD, then apply the retention BACKUP_KEEP_DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY (7/4/6). Keep that password offline: without it the off-host copies are useless, with it they are the keys to everything --list List local backups. With --offsite, list the restic snapshots; --json prints restic's JSON

items.title: backup verify
items.text:
portcullis backup verify [--snapshot ID]
portcullis backup verify --local [DIR]

Off-host (default). Runs restic check, reading BACKUP_VERIFY_READ_DATA (default 10%) of the pack data. Then it restores the latest snapshot (or ID) into a temporary directory and checks it.

--local. Checks a local backup instead: DIR, by default the newest in backups/.

The checks:

  • every file matches MANIFEST.json, and .env / secrets/ are complete
  • vault.snap is a raft snapshot (meta.json, state.bin, SHA256SUMS ok)
  • postgres.dump restores into a throwaway Postgres container (no network) and contains the Keycloak realms
  • the LLDAP database opens, passes integrity_check and has users
  • every volume archive is readable

Exits non-zero if anything fails.

items.title: backup schedule
items.text:
portcullis backup schedule --systemd [--on-calendar SPEC] [--output DIR]

Prints, or writes to DIR, a systemd service and timer. They run portcullis backup --offsite (just backup while BACKUP_REPOSITORY is unset) as the current user, followed by portcullis status --textfile. The user must be able to run docker.

Option Meaning --systemd Generate systemd units (the only scheduler supported) --on-calendar SPEC systemd OnCalendar (default *-*-* 03:15:00, plus up to 30 minutes random delay) --output DIR Write portcullis-backup.service / .timer into DIR and print the install commands

items.title: restore
items.text:
portcullis restore [--yes] <backup-dir>
portcullis restore [--yes] --from-offsite [SNAPSHOT]
portcullis restore --list [--offsite]

Stops Portcullis and restores a backup made by portcullis backup or upgrade:

  • .env, certs/, secrets/ and the config files
  • the Vault data: the raft snapshot is restored into a fresh Vault, which then unseals with the backed-up key
  • the Keycloak database: pg_restore into a fresh Postgres
  • the LLDAP, Hub and ACME volumes

Then everything is started again. The backup's checksums are verified first. The current .env, secrets/ and certs/ are saved to backups/pre-restore-<timestamp>/.

--from-offsite restores SNAPSHOT (default: latest) from BACKUP_REPOSITORY. On a new host without .env, export BACKUP_REPOSITORY, BACKUP_PASSWORD and the provider credentials first. The .env comes from the backup.

Option Meaning -y, --yes Do not ask for confirmation --from-offsite Restore from the restic repository --list List local backups (--offsite: restic snapshots)

items.title: config apply
items.text:
portcullis config apply [--bundle-only]

Applies the TLS toggles in .env and rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt:

Variable Default Effect ACME_STAGING=true\|false false Let's Encrypt staging vs production. Sets ACME_CA_SERVER in .env. On a flip it clears Traefik's acme.json so Traefik registers again MTLS_ENABLED=true\|false true Rewrites traefik/dynamic/tls.yml. With false no tier requests client certs, and routers that rely only on the protected tier become unauthenticated

Run portcullis up afterwards to restart Traefik. See TLS & mTLS.

Option Meaning --bundle-only Only rebuild certs/ca-bundle.crt (system CAs + internal PKI chain + the LE staging root if ACME_STAGING=true)

items.title: config init
items.text:
portcullis config init [--remote URL | --from URL]

Creates config/, a separate git repo for this instance's settings. It moves .env, docker-compose.override.yml and traefik/dynamic/local/*.yml into it and symlinks them back, so a git pull of Portcullis never conflicts with your settings. Re-running it only refreshes the symlinks.

Option Meaning --remote URL Set config/'s git remote. Push it to a private repo: .env holds secrets --from URL Clone an existing config repo into config/ (new machine)

items.title: dns setup
items.text:
portcullis dns setup [--check]

Creates or updates the A records (and AAAA, if the host has public IPv6) for PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN and *.PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN. They point at this host's public IP. It uses DNS_PROVIDER and the provider's credentials from .env:

Provider Variables cloudflare CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN porkbun PORKBUN_API_KEY, PORKBUN_SECRET_API_KEY digitalocean DO_AUTH_TOKEN hetzner HETZNER_API_KEY route53 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_HOSTED_ZONE_ID (needs the aws CLI)

For other providers, or none, it prints the records to create by hand.

Option Meaning --check Only compare what resolves (via 1.1.1.1) with the public IP. Exits non-zero if the records are not correct yet

See DNS Configuration.

items.title: vault init
items.text:
portcullis vault init

Idempotent. It is run by portcullis init, upgrade and restore.

  1. Starts the vault container if it is not running.
  2. If Vault is uninitialised, runs vault operator init with one key share. The output goes to secrets/vault-init.json (0600). The unseal key goes to secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key (0640, group of the vault user). That file is mounted read-only into vault, which auto-unseals on every start.
  3. Unseals Vault if it is sealed and waits until the raft node is active.
  4. Enables AppRole and writes the portcullis-enroll policy (vault/policies/enroll.hcl) and role. The enroll role-id and secret-id go to secrets/enroll/ (0640, group 10002 = the enroll user), which is mounted read-only into enroll.
  5. Writes the portcullis-metrics policy (vault/policies/metrics.hcl: read sys/metrics) and keeps a token with only that policy in secrets/monitoring/prometheus/vault-token for Prometheus (monitoring profile). The token is recreated when it has less than a year left.

Keep an offline copy of secrets/vault-init.json

Losing it together with the host means losing the CA.

items.title: vault unseal
items.text:
portcullis vault unseal

Unseals Vault with secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key if it is sealed. Vault normally does this itself on every container start. Then it waits until Vault is the active raft node, and exits non-zero if that doesn't happen.

items.title: vault rotate-enroll-secret
items.text:
portcullis vault rotate-enroll-secret

Same as portcullis vault init, but it always issues a new enroll AppRole secret-id (secrets/enroll/secret-id) and destroys every previous one. The enroll service picks it up on its next login.

items.title: pki setup
items.text:
portcullis pki setup [--force] [--with-server-cert]

Creates the client-certificate CA in Vault:

  • root CA (10 years) and intermediate CA (5 years)
  • the client-cert role, with lifetime CLIENT_CERT_TTL (default 720h = 30 days). The CN is taken from the caller, never from the CSR

It writes certs/root-ca.crt, intermediate-ca.crt, ca-chain.crt and Keycloak's truststore (certs/truststore/portcullis-ca-chain.pem), and enables CRL auto-rebuild on pki_int.

It is idempotent:

  • An existing CA is never replaced.
  • The client-cert role is rewritten, so a new CLIENT_CERT_TTL applies to certs issued from then on.
  • Missing pieces (CA files, truststore, server cert) are recreated.
  • A partial earlier run is redone.

If Vault has no CA but certs/ca-chain.crt exists (Vault data lost), it refuses to create a new CA. Restore a backup, or use --force.

Option Meaning --force Destroy the existing CA and create a new one. Every enrolled client certificate stops working --with-server-cert Also issue a self-signed *.<domain> server cert (certs/server.crt, server.key 0640 group 0) for local dev and CI

Admin token: VAULT_TOKEN if set, else the root token in secrets/vault-init.json.

items.title: keycloak configure
items.text:
portcullis keycloak configure [--wipe-realm]

Idempotent configuration of the portcullis realm after start, through the admin API on 127.0.0.1:8080 (override with KEYCLOAK_URL):

  • imports keycloak/realm-export.json if the realm does not exist
  • points the LDAP federation at LLDAP (LLDAP_BASE_DN, LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD)
  • sets the ACR→LoA map and browserFlow=portcullis-universal
  • pushes the X.509 authenticator settings from the file to the realm: CRL check against Vault's pki_int CRL, trust re-validation, clientAuth EKU
  • checks the AMR reference values, and ensures the amr mapper and the groups scope
  • ensures the email-unverified scope (email claim, no email_verified) that Hub templates opt into with keycloak_clients[].email_verified_claim: false
  • sets the acr/groups scopes and the redirect URI on portcullis-forward-auth
  • creates a credential-less testuser and applies the PORTAL_DISPLAY_NAME branding
Option Meaning --wipe-realm Delete the realm first and re-import it from the file. Needed to apply auth-flow changes; clients must then be re-registered with portcullis oidc register

items.title: oidc register
items.text:
portcullis oidc register

Creates the portcullis-forward-auth client. It also creates headscale, headplane and netbird-dashboard when their *_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET is set in .env. Each client's secret in Keycloak is set to the value in .env, so oauth2-proxy and Keycloak always agree. Idempotent.

After changing FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, run this, then portcullis up.

items.title: invite
items.text:
portcullis invite <user> [--ttl DURATION] [--to hub|portal|URL] [--replace-keys] [--json]

Prints a one-time setup link for an LLDAP user. Opening it lets the user register a passkey or security key (YubiKey) and signs them in: no password, no other step. The link is single use, expires after --ttl (default 72h, max 168h) and replaces the user's previous links. Pending links do not survive a restart of the enroll container.

This is also how the bootstrap admin gets (or recovers) its key: the Hub refuses invites for admin; only the server can issue them.

Option Meaning --ttl DURATION Go duration, e.g. 30m, 24h --to Where to land afterwards: hub (https://hub.<domain>/), portal (https://<domain>/, default) or an https URL on the domain --replace-keys Lost or stolen key: first delete all of the user's passkeys and security keys in Keycloak and sign them out everywhere. Without it the new key is added next to the old ones (a spare key) --json Print enroll's JSON ({"url","expires_at"})

items.title: lldap-ui
items.text:
portcullis lldap-ui

Break-glass access to LLDAP's own web UI. directory.<domain> redirects to people.<domain> (LLDAP has no single sign-on), so LLDAP's UI is reachable only from the server. The command prints the SSH tunnel to run on your machine; then open http://localhost:17170 and sign in as the LLDAP admin (LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env). Use it for recovery only: day-to-day, people and groups are managed in the Hub at hub.<domain> (admins) or people.<domain> (everyone, with per-request permission checks). Manual changes to rule-based groups in LLDAP are reverted by the Hub's evaluator and audited.

items.title: Client certificates (YubiKey PIV)
items.text:
cert enroll and cert renew need ykman, openssl, jq and Vault access. Run them on the Portcullis host, or export VAULT_ADDR/VAULT_TOKEN. The cert CN is <username>.

Environment Meaning PIV_PIN YubiKey PIV PIN. If unset, ykman prompts for it. Prompting is preferred, because a PIN given here appears on the ykman command line VAULT_TOKEN Admin token (default: root token from secrets/vault-init.json) VAULT_ADDR Default http://127.0.0.1:8200

items.title: cert enroll
items.text:
portcullis cert enroll [--slot SLOT] [--ttl TTL] <username> [email]

Generates a new ECCP256 key pair on the YubiKey, overwriting the slot. It then creates a CSR, has Vault sign it, and imports the certificate into the slot.

Option Meaning --slot SLOT PIV slot (default: $PIV_SLOT or 9a, Authentication) --ttl TTL Certificate lifetime (default: $CLIENT_CERT_TTL or 720h). The Vault role caps it at CLIENT_CERT_TTL as of the last pki setup

items.title: cert renew
items.text:
portcullis cert renew [--slot SLOT] [--ttl TTL] <username> [email]

Keeps the key already on the YubiKey and issues a fresh certificate for it. Same options as cert enroll. Users can also renew their own certificate at https://enroll.<domain>/self (see TLS & mTLS).

items.title: cert revoke
items.text:
portcullis cert revoke [--yes] <serial>

Revokes a client certificate in Vault and rewrites the revoked-serial list that group-gate checks on every request. Find serials with portcullis cert list or in the enrollment UI (/certs).

Option Meaning -y, --yes Do not ask for confirmation

items.title: cert list
items.text:
portcullis cert list [--all]

Lists issued client certificates: serial, CN, status and expiry. expiring means fewer than CERT_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS (default 7) days are left.

Option Meaning --all Include revoked certificates

items.title: cert sync
items.text:
portcullis cert sync

Rewrites certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt atomically from Vault's list of revoked serials. If Vault cannot be queried (sealed, bad token, unreachable), the file is left unchanged and the command fails. It never "un-revokes" by writing an empty list.

items.title: Groups & Access Control
items.text: Portcullis uses LLDAP groups to control which users can access which apps. Groups can be manual (membership managed by hand) or rule-based (computed from custom user fields). This page explains the group model, rule-based groups, how groups flow through the system, and how to manage access.

items.title: The Group Model
items.text:
Every app in Portcullis has two associated LLDAP groups:

Group Pattern Purpose Access group users_<app> Grants access to the app. Users not in this group get a 403 from group-gate. Admin group admin_<app> Grants admin privileges within the app (if the app supports group-based admin).

For example, Jellyfin has:

  • users_jellyfin -- Members can access Jellyfin
  • admin_jellyfin -- Members get Jellyfin admin privileges

These group names are defined in each app's manifest.yaml under auth.access_group and auth.admin_group.

items.title: Manual vs. Rule-Based Groups
items.text:
• Manual groups: membership is managed directly by admins (add/remove members, set expiries).
  • Rule-based groups: membership is computed by the Hub from custom user fields (department, office, manager, etc.). Rules combine conditions (all/any blocks) and can reference any field. The Hub evaluates rules at least every 60 seconds and on every relevant change (details, rules, exceptions, import).

Groups are ordinary LLDAP groups; apps, group-gate and Keycloak use them the same way whether manual or rule-based.

items.title: Rule-Based Groups
items.text: Rule-based groups grant membership automatically based on who people are, not by hand-picking members. Example rules: "everyone in the Milan office gets Nextcloud", "anyone reporting to Anna can see Grafana". The Hub evaluates rules continuously and updates LLDAP membership.

items.title: Creating a Rule
items.text:
Admins can make a group rule-based in the Hub's Groups tab. Rules are edited two ways that stay in sync:

  1. Blocks (default): point-and-click all/any blocks, nestable. Conditions: is, is not, is one of (list fields), is empty, and for person fields (e.g. manager) reports to (directly or indirectly).
  2. Text rule: a typed expression with autocomplete for field names and list values, plus inline errors. A toggle switches between them; a parse error refuses the toggle.

A preview shows who matches (count and names, live-updated while editing).

Converting a manual group to rule-based: opens a review. Current members who don't match the rule are pre-ticked to stay as "added" exceptions (reason: "member before the rule (set by X on date)"). Untick whoever should leave. Nothing changes until confirmed. The Hub compares the review with a fresh preview inside its lock and refuses with 409 if they differ (someone added/removed in between) — convert again.

items.title: Exceptions
items.text:
On a rule-based group, admins can:

  • Add someone although the rule doesn't match them (they stay even if the rule changes), or
  • Keep out someone although the rule matches (the evaluator skips them).

Each exception needs a written reason (≤ 500 characters, shown to everyone) and may have an expiry (date/time; they're removed automatically when it arrives). An expired exception is kept (still denying for "kept out", doing nothing for "added" once the person left the group) until the person's membership changes or an admin deletes it.

items.title: Expiries
items.text:
• Manual groups: admins can set an expiry on any membership (date/time; removed automatically).
  • Rule-based groups: use exceptions with expiries. Direct Add/Remove is not offered (the evaluator would revert it).
  • Built-in groups (lldap_admin): expiries are refused (409).

When a membership expires, the Hub removes it from LLDAP, revokes the user's Keycloak sessions (OIDC apps lose access at their next token refresh, within ~1 minute), and keeps the expiry in the policy file's expiring array (plus a 10-minute grace period) so enforcement is strict even while the Hub is down. When group-gate withholds an expired membership for a request, it also withholds Authorization and X-Forwarded-Access-Token.

items.title: The Evaluator
items.text:
The Hub runs the rule evaluator:

  • at least every 60 seconds (cadence),
  • immediately on every detail change, rule change, exception change, CSV import that affects membership, and on expiries.

For each rule-based group (skipping administrator and built-in groups):

  1. Computes who matches the rule (handles cycles in the manager field: reports to stops at the first repeat).
  2. Applies exceptions (adds "added" exceptions, skips "kept out" exceptions).
  3. Compares with LLDAP membership and updates it (adds/removes members).
  4. Audits every change (group.rule_add, group.rule_remove, group.expired) with the cause.

The Hub owns rule-group membership. A manual change made in LLDAP to a rule-based group (e.g. in portcullis lldap-ui) is reverted at the next evaluation and audited as group.manual_change_reverted.

items.title: Guarding Groups
items.text:
Rules of protected groups may only reference admin-only fields:

  • Administrator groups: lldap_admin, lldap_password_manager, core-subdomain groups (auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, people, metrics), INVITE_PROTECTED_GROUPS
  • Permission groups: the groups holding a delegated permission (edit_details, invite, remove)
  • App admin groups: any group used as an app's admin_group or in path_groups

This prevents delegates (who can edit non-admin-only fields) from granting themselves admin rights or delegated permissions by editing data. A field used by such a rule cannot lose its admin-only flag (409 until the rule is changed or the group stops being protected).

Built-in groups (lldap_admin, lldap_password_manager, core-subdomain groups) and permission groups cannot be rule-based (409). INVITE_PROTECTED_GROUPS can be rule-based, but only over admin-only fields.

items.title: Membership Flow for Rule-Based Groups
items.text:
1. Fields: admins define custom fields (department, office, manager) under Setup in the Hub. Admins and delegates (with edit_details permission) fill in values.
  2. Rules: admins write a rule that combines conditions over those fields.
  3. Evaluator: the Hub runs the rule every ≤ 60 s and on changes, computes who matches, applies exceptions, updates LLDAP membership.
  4. Sync: Keycloak syncs groups from LLDAP periodically (and can be triggered manually).
  5. Access: apps enforce group membership the same way as manual groups (group-gate for the subdomain's access_group, the app's own group-admin mapping for admin_group).

items.title: How Groups Flow
items.text:
Groups originate in LLDAP and flow through the system:

LLDAP (source of truth)
  |
  v  LDAP federation (periodic sync)
Keycloak (identity provider)
  |
  v  OIDC groups claim
oauth2-proxy (forward auth)
  |
  v  X-Auth-Request-Groups header
group-gate (access check)
  |
  v  subdomain -> required group mapping
App (allowed or denied)

items.title: Step by step:
items.text:
1. LLDAP stores users and groups. An admin creates groups and assigns users to them.
  2. Keycloak federates from LLDAP via its LDAP user storage provider. Groups are synced periodically (and can be triggered manually).
  3. oauth2-proxy authenticates users via Keycloak's OIDC endpoint. The ID token includes a groups claim with the user's LLDAP groups.
  4. group-gate receives the X-Auth-Request-Groups header (set by oauth2-proxy) and checks whether the user belongs to the required group for the requested subdomain.

items.title: group-gate and the Subdomain Map
items.text:
group-gate is the forward-auth service behind the portcullis-groups@docker middleware. It maps subdomains to required groups. Two sources are merged, and both are re-read on every request:

  1. group-gate/group-gate-map.conf in the core repo (mounted read-only into group-gate) holds static entries, mainly for the core services:

    # subdomain=required_group
auth=lldap_admin
hub=lldap_admin
grafana=users_grafana

    Edits take effect on the next request; no restart is needed.

  2. The Hub's group-gate-policy.json (version 3, on the hub_data volume) has a groups map. The Hub rewrites it whenever an app is enabled, disabled or reconfigured. For every enabled template with auth.group_access: true, each subdomain the template routes maps to the manifest's auth.access_group. For example, Nextcloud routes cloud.<domain> and declares users_nextcloud, so it yields cloud = users_nextcloud. Hub entries add to or override the map file for app subdomains.

Keys are subdomains only. Policies, groups and path rules are never keyed by template ID, because an ID could equal another app's subdomain. The Hub refuses to enable a template that routes a subdomain another enabled app already routes, and rejects templates whose Host() rules it can't fully resolve (see Hub → Template rules).

Core subdomains (auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, metrics) always come from the map file. The Hub never publishes them, and group-gate ignores them in the policy file. If they are missing from the map file they default to lldap_admin.

items.title: What group-gate checks
items.text:
When a request for grafana.<domain> arrives, group-gate runs these checks in order and stops at the first failure:

  1. Host. It takes the host from X-Forwarded-Host, lowercases it, and strips any port and trailing dot. The host must be exactly <label>.<PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN>; anything else gets a 403. Traefik matches hosts case-insensitively, so without normalisation HUB.<domain> would miss the hub entry.
  2. Reserved group. A user whose groups include __portcullis_deny__ is denied.
  3. Revocation. If the request carries a client certificate (via client-headers@file, which must come before portcullis-groups@docker), its serial must not be revoked. See TLS & mTLS.
  4. Auth policy. If the app has a policy (or there is a global default), the session's acr/amr must satisfy it. Otherwise group-gate returns the step-up page. Policies satisfied only through mtls also need the current request's certificate to match the user (mTLS binding). See Authentication Policies.
  5. Group. It looks up the subdomain's required group (users_grafana) and compares it with X-Auth-Request-Groups (set by oauth2-proxy). The header is split on commas only, and the match must be exact.
  6. Path rules. If the subdomain has path_groups, the group of the matching path rule is required in addition (see below).
  7. Allow. It returns 200 OK and sets X-Forwarded-User / X-Auth-Request-User (the LLDAP username), X-Forwarded-Email / X-Auth-Request-Email and X-Auth-Request-Groups for the backend. Identity is always the immutable LLDAP username, never the user-editable email. Apps must never create, match or link accounts by email. Otherwise it returns 403 Forbidden.

Fail closed. These all deny the request instead of falling back to "public":

  • a policy file that exists but can't be parsed
  • a version newer than group-gate understands
  • an unknown factor, op or rule shape

If a subdomain has no mapping at all, group-gate allows any authenticated user and logs ALLOW-UNMAPPED. This is the passthrough for apps without group-based access.

items.title: The reserved group __portcullis_deny__
items.text:
The Hub publishes groups[sub] = "__portcullis_deny__" for subdomains it knows are routed but can't attribute a config to. That happens when:

  • an enabled app has neither a template nor a stored snapshot
  • a portcullis-<id> project runs without being enabled

Nobody is a member of that group, so every request to those subdomains is denied ("The configuration of … is unavailable"). A user who claims membership is denied everywhere.

Never create an LLDAP group named __portcullis_deny__

Membership would be treated as tampering and deny that user on every app.

See Hub → Fail-closed behaviour.

items.title: Path rules (path_groups and admin_paths)
items.text:
Some apps keep an admin area on a path of the same subdomain, e.g. Vaultwarden's /admin. A template lists such prefixes in its manifest:

auth:
  admin_group: admin_vaultwarden
  admin_paths: ["/admin"]

For every subdomain of an enabled template, the Hub publishes path_groups[sub] = [{"prefix": "/admin", "group": "admin_vaultwarden"}]. On requests under that prefix, group-gate then requires admin_group in addition to the subdomain's group.

Matching:

  • What is matched. The path from X-Forwarded-Uri with the query and fragment stripped. It is percent-decoded once, // is collapsed, and dot segments (/./, /../) are resolved.
  • Ambiguous paths are denied. If an encoded slash, backslash or NUL (%2F, %5C, %00) is still present after that one decode, or the path has control characters, the request is denied outright. Different backends read such paths differently.
  • Deny-biased variants. A rule applies if it matches any of: the primary form, the fully decoded form, \ read as /, ; path parameters stripped. Each is compared both case-sensitively and case-insensitively. So /%61dmin, //admin, /x/../admin and /ADMIN all hit the /admin rule (CI's browser test checks exactly these).
  • Segment-boundary prefixes. /admin matches /admin and /admin/x, but not /administrator. The longest matching prefix wins. If different variants hit rules with different groups, all of those groups are required.

Only routers with group-gate are covered

Path rules only work on routers whose middlewares include portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker. For a native-OIDC app, the template routes the admin path through its own higher-priority PathPrefix router with forward-auth (validate.py in the templates repo checks that such a router exists).

items.title: /authenticated: any signed-in user
items.text: group-gate also serves /authenticated, used by the core middleware portcullis-self@docker. It runs every check except the subdomain group check (step 5): host, revocation, policy, path rules, and a signed-in user. Core uses it for enroll.<domain>/self, where every user may renew their own certificate without being in lldap_admin.

items.title: Per-App Enforcement
items.text: How group access is enforced depends on the auth method:

items.title: Forward-Auth and Header-Auth Apps
items.text:
The Traefik middleware chain handles everything:

client-headers@file --> portcullis-auth@docker --> portcullis-groups@docker --> App
(client cert info)      (oauth2-proxy)             (group-gate)

Both oauth2-proxy and group-gate run as Traefik forward-auth middleware. The app itself is unaware of groups (header-auth apps receive them in X-Auth-Request-Groups).

items.title: Native OIDC Apps
items.text:
Native OIDC apps receive the user's groups in the groups claim (the Hub attaches the groups client scope to every client it registers). Some apps enforce group-based access themselves, e.g. Jellyfin's SSO plugin requires users_jellyfin and maps admin_jellyfin to admin. Each app page in the App Catalog says what it does.

Apps that can't restrict OIDC logins by group (GitLab, LiteLLM, Vaultwarden) put only their interactive login paths behind forward-auth + group-gate on a higher-priority PathPrefix router, and keep their API router without forward-auth. Never put portcullis-auth@docker on the host-wide router of a native-OIDC app: it would break API clients and mobile apps.

items.title: Public Apps
items.text: No group enforcement. Anyone can access the app.

items.title: Creating Groups
items.text:
Groups are created in the Hub's Groups tab:

  • Admins: https://hub.<your-domain> → Users & Groups tab → Groups section

  • Everyone: https://people.<your-domain> (read-only for non-admins)

  • Under Groups, enter the group name (e.g., users_grafana) and click Create. New groups are manual.

  • Groups an enabled app needs but that don't exist yet are listed under Missing groups, each with a one-click Create.

https://directory.<your-domain> redirects to https://people.<your-domain>. LLDAP has no single sign-on, so its own web UI isn't published; for recovery, open it from the server with portcullis lldap-ui.

items.title: Adding Users to Groups
items.text:
Manual groups: In the Hub's Groups tab (admins only), expand the group and use Add member / Remove member. Adding someone to an administrator group asks for confirmation.

Rule-based groups: membership is computed. To include someone, either adjust the rule or add them as an "added" exception (with a reason). To exclude someone the rule matches, add a "kept out" exception.

items.title: Syncing Groups to Keycloak
items.text:
Keycloak syncs groups from LLDAP periodically. To trigger an immediate sync:

  1. Open Keycloak admin at https://auth.<your-domain>/admin/
  2. Go to User Federation
  3. Click on the LLDAP provider
  4. Click Synchronize all users

Or via API:

# Get admin token
KC_TOKEN=$(curl -s http://localhost:8080/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token \
  -d "client_id=admin-cli" \
  -d "username=admin" \
  -d "password=YOUR_KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
  -d "grant_type=password" | jq -r '.access_token')

# Find LDAP provider ID
LDAP_ID=$(curl -s http://localhost:8080/admin/realms/portcullis/components \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KC_TOKEN" | jq -r '.[] | select(.providerId=="ldap") | .id')

# Trigger full sync
curl -s -X POST \
  "http://localhost:8080/admin/realms/portcullis/user-storage/$LDAP_ID/sync?action=triggerFullSync" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KC_TOKEN"

items.title: Example: Giving a User Access to an App
items.text:
To give user alice access to Grafana:

  1. Create the users_grafana group in LLDAP if it doesn't exist yet (the Hub does not create groups)
  2. Add alice to the users_grafana group in LLDAP
  3. Wait for Keycloak sync (or trigger manually)
  4. alice can now access https://grafana.<your-domain>

To also give alice admin privileges in Grafana, add her to admin_grafana.

items.title: Example: Revoking Access
items.text:
To revoke alice's access to Grafana:

  1. Remove alice from the users_grafana group in LLDAP
  2. Trigger a Keycloak sync
  3. alice will receive a 403 on her next request (after her oauth2-proxy session expires)

Tip

oauth2-proxy sessions have a configurable expiry. For immediate revocation, you can also revoke the user's Keycloak sessions from the Keycloak admin panel.

items.title: Security & Hardening
items.text: This page covers what the core stack (docker-compose.yml in the core repo) does to limit the damage a compromised component can do, and where it can't: the threat model, network layout, Docker socket proxies, per-service container settings, the secrets containers read, and header trust.

items.title: Threat model summary
items.text:
Asset / boundary Threat Mitigation Logins Phishing, password reuse WebAuthn (FIDO2) and PIV client certificates. Both are bound to the origin or the TLS handshake. Per-app policies can require them User identity A user changes their own LLDAP email to someone else's Identity is the immutable username everywhere; email is never used to authorise or link accounts Identity headers (X-Forwarded-User, client-cert headers) Spoofed by an internet client Traefik deletes client-supplied X-Forwarded-* and cert headers on the entrypoint, and forward-auth replaces the identity headers Attribute headers (X-Forwarded-Attr-*) Spoofed by an internet client or by routers without forwardAuth Client copies stripped by authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr- on every forwardAuth middleware (Traefik can't delete headers by prefix in a headers middleware). Routers without forwardAuth (keycloak, vault-ui, enroll-invite, headscale, netbird, docs) don't strip them; backends there must not trust them Identity headers Spoofed by another container on portcullis-proxy Header-auth apps trust only Traefik's fixed IP (PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP). Keycloak trusts proxy headers only from Traefik's fixed IP on the internal portcullis-auth network Hub (runs compose, so it is effectively host root) Reached without passing forward-auth Hub: requires lldap_admin and the X-Portcullis-Proxy-Secret header. People listener (people.<domain>): any signed-in user (group-gate-map.conf people=*), per-request permission checks Docker API A compromised Traefik or Hub takes over the host No service mounts the socket except two socket proxies with per-client allow-lists Lost or stolen YubiKey cert Keeps working until expiry Revocation is checked on every request (group-gate), at Keycloak X.509 login (CRL, fail closed), and by the mTLS binding. On removal or expiry, group-gate also withholds Authorization and X-Forwarded-Access-Token Expired group membership Keeps working while Hub is down Every pending expiry is in the policy file's expiring array (plus a 10-min grace after LLDAP removal). group-gate treats it as absent. The Hub also revokes Keycloak sessions (oauth2-proxy cookie refresh is 1 min, so removals and Keycloak logouts take effect within ~1 min; sessions end at Keycloak's idle 8h / max 12h) Path-based admin areas Bypassed with encoded or dot-segment paths group-gate normalises the path and denies ambiguous encodings (see Groups) Templates (outside contributions) A malicious or careless template opens access The Hub rejects routing it can't fully see, refuses subdomain collisions and core subdomains, validates custom overrides (no Traefik labels, host-path bind roots, privileges), and fails closed on unknown config. Templates CI lints fork PRs without secrets Public exceptions (share links, off unless an admin turns them on) Anonymous access to app endpoints, token guessing, share-password brute force, identity spoofing on header-auth apps Only declared, validated prefixes; listed mode routes only admin-listed share tokens; identity headers stripped; rate-limit@file; see Public exceptions Vault data volume Copied off the host Encrypted. The unseal key is in secrets/ on the host, so a copy of the volume alone is useless Host root / docker group Full compromise Out of scope. Anyone who can run docker is root-equivalent, and the unseal key is on the host

Known limits:

  • The Hub can still start arbitrary containers (privileged, host mounts): that is what "run compose for any template" means. Treat it as host root.
  • Auto-unseal trades confidentiality at rest for availability on the same host (see TLS & mTLS).
  • Routers without portcullis-groups@docker don't get revocation checks. They also get no group or path checks.

items.title: Public exceptions
items.text:
An app's public exceptions are the one place where Portcullis deliberately lets unauthenticated internet traffic reach an app. What a turned-on exception exposes:

  • Every endpoint under each opened prefix, to anyone, without login, group, hardware key or policy. Only the app's own checks remain (share token, share password, expiry, download limits). In mode all that includes guessing share tokens; in mode listed only the listed shares are routed, and any other token on the same prefix still goes through forward-auth.
  • The app's share-password form (e.g. Nextcloud /s/<token>/authenticate) to brute force. Only the app's own brute-force protection and Traefik's rate-limit@file (50 req/s average, burst 100, per client IP) limit it. The app must see the real client IP (e.g. Nextcloud's TRUSTED_PROXIES = Traefik) or its limiter locks out everyone at once.
  • Static files under supporting paths (assets, l10n, theming; matched by extension, e.g. Grafana /public/plugins reveals installed plugins), and the few exact routes a template justifies. A front controller that routes extension-suffixed paths to code (Nextcloud's /apps/theming/theme/<id>.css, /core/js/oc.js) still runs those #[PublicPage] routes.
  • Uploads where the app allows them on a share (Nextcloud file drop via /public.php/dav).
  • The host's TLS tier. With an mTLS-only policy the host drops from protected@file to authaware@file: group-gate still enforces the client certificate per request on gated routers, but native-OIDC apps then check it only at login (Keycloak acr), and routers without group-gate not at all.

What it can't do:

  • reach paths outside the prefixes: the router matches Path(p) / PathPrefix(p/) on Traefik's sanitised path (dot-segments resolved), so /s/x/../../apps/files is matched as /apps/files and stays gated;
  • overlap admin paths, login gates or other routers of the app (the Hub refuses the template), or /admin, /oauth2, /.well-known;
  • carry an identity: X-Forwarded-User, X-Forwarded-Email, the other forward-auth headers, Remote-* and the template's identity_headers (and their _ forms) are deleted, so a header-auth app (Grafana) can't be told who the visitor is;
  • carry a login past the hardware key: core's public guard (group-gate /public-guard, first middleware of every public router) answers 403 to requests with Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, the template's credential_headers, credential_cookies or credential_query. Cookie and query names are normalised the way PHP does (php-src php_register_variable_ex: leading spaces, /. → _, name[…], NUL), raw and percent-decoded, case-insensitively; non-UTF-8 names are refused. It also denies any path outside the published patterns, a #, and encoded /, \, NUL or #. A plain session cookie the template doesn't list (Nextcloud's oc<instanceid>, needed for share passwords and CSRF) is passed; it only reaches share-scoped routes and static files there;
  • be opened by a template on its own: the Hub generates the router, only while an admin (or a template default that opens nothing until an admin lists a share) has it on, and reports any running exposure label that differs from what it would render as drift.

Trade-off: an app user signed in with a remember-me cookie gets the guard's 403 on a public link in the same browser (open it in a private window). The guard serves only version 4 of the policy file, so the Hub and core are upgraded together.

Not everything with a share feature can be scoped: Vaultwarden Send needs the web vault at / and the password-login token endpoint, and Kanboard's router reads ?controller= before the path, so neither declares public exceptions.

items.title: Networks
items.text:
Each box is a service; each hexagon is a Docker network. A line means "is attached to".

graph LR
    Internet((Internet)) -->|:80 / :443| T[Traefik]

    NP{{portcullis-proxy<br/>fixed IPAM, Traefik .2}}
    NA{{portcullis-auth<br/>internal, fixed IPAM}}
    NC{{portcullis<br/>core}}
    NST{{socket-proxy-traefik<br/>internal}}
    NSH{{socket-proxy-hub<br/>internal}}

    T --- NP
    T --- NA
    T --- NC
    T --- NST
    Apps[App frontends] --- NP
    Apps --- AppNet{{one per app: portcullis-APP_default}}
    AppDB[(App databases)] --- AppNet
    KC[Keycloak] --- NA
    KC --- NC
    O2[oauth2-proxy] --- NC
    GG[group-gate] --- NC
    En[enroll] --- NC
    V[Vault] --- NC
    LL[LLDAP] --- NC
    PG[(PostgreSQL)] --- NC
    Hub --- NC
    Hub --- NSH
    SPT[socket-proxy-traefik] --- NST
    SPH[socket-proxy-hub] --- NSH
    SPT -->|read-only API| Sock[(docker.sock)]
    SPH -->|compose API subset| Sock
Network Members Addressing Purpose portcullis Traefik and all core services Docker default Core service traffic: forward-auth, Vault, LLDAP, PostgreSQL portcullis-proxy Traefik and app frontends PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET (default 172.31.250.0/24). Dynamic range PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE (172.31.250.128/25). Traefik pinned at PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP (172.31.250.2), outside the range Routing plane. Traefik's docker provider uses this network. No app container can ever get Traefik's address portcullis-auth Traefik and Keycloak only (internal: true) PORTCULLIS_AUTH_SUBNET (172.31.251.0/28), range PORTCULLIS_AUTH_IP_RANGE (172.31.251.8/29), Traefik at PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP (172.31.251.2) The only path from which Keycloak accepts proxy headers, including the forwarded client cert for X.509 login socket-proxy-traefik Traefik + its socket proxy (internal: true) Docker default Read-only Docker API for Traefik socket-proxy-hub Hub + its socket proxy (internal: true) Docker default Docker API for the Hub monitoring (profile monitoring, internal: true) Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, blackbox, textfile exporter Docker default Scraping and dashboards. Prometheus and blackbox also join portcullis, Grafana joins portcullis-proxy (routed at metrics.<domain>) alerting (profile monitoring) Alertmanager Docker default Alertmanager's only network with egress, for the receivers portcullis-<app>_default One app's services Docker default App-internal traffic (databases, caches). Isolated from other apps and from core

CI checks that exactly keycloak and traefik are on portcullis-auth, and that each socket-proxy network has exactly its two members.

Changing the ranges. Only do this if the defaults collide with a host, LAN or VPN network, ideally before ./portcullis init. The rules:

  • the IP range must be inside its subnet
  • the range must not contain the Traefik IP
  • the two subnets must not overlap

./portcullis up and upgrade validate them and refuse to run when an existing network has different IPAM:

  • portcullis-proxy: disable the apps in the Hub, ./portcullis down, docker network rm portcullis-proxy, ./portcullis up, then re-enable the apps so their env picks up the new Traefik IP.
  • portcullis-auth (core only): ./portcullis down && ./portcullis up.

items.title: Docker socket proxies
items.text:
No service mounts /var/run/docker.sock except two linuxserver/socket-proxy containers (HAProxy, pinned by digest). Each sits on its own internal network, shared with exactly one client (integration contract §6):

Proxy Client Network Allowed API sections (1) Methods socket-proxy-traefik Traefik (TRAEFIK_PROVIDERS_DOCKER_ENDPOINT=tcp://socket-proxy-traefik:2375) socket-proxy-traefik CONTAINERS, NETWORKS, EVENTS, VERSION, PING GET/HEAD only (POST=0) socket-proxy-hub Hub (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://socket-proxy-hub:2375) socket-proxy-hub CONTAINERS, IMAGES, NETWORKS, VOLUMES, EXEC, EVENTS, INFO, VERSION, PING, ALLOW_LOGS All. POST=1 also allows PUT/DELETE on the allowed sections

The Hub's set is what docker compose up/down/ps/logs and the Hub's own Engine API calls (status, logs, exec, events) need:

  • containers: create, start, stop, kill, rm, inspect, list, wait, logs, exec
  • images: pull (/images/create) and inspect
  • networks and volumes: create, inspect, rm
  • /events, /info, /version, /_ping

Everything else is denied: BUILD, COMMIT, SWARM, NODES, SERVICES, TASKS, SECRETS, CONFIGS, PLUGINS, SYSTEM (df / prune), AUTH, DISTRIBUTION, SESSION, and container archive / export. CI runs a real docker compose project through socket-proxy-hub and checks the denials.

Limits of a socket proxy. The Hub can still create containers with any HostConfig (privileged, host bind mounts): that is inherent to "runs compose for arbitrary templates". The proxy removes the rest of the API surface (swarm, plugins, image builds, system prune, secrets). Treat the Hub as host-root-equivalent and keep it behind lldap_admin and the proxy secret.

items.title: Container hardening
items.text:
Every core service gets:

  • security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] and cap_drop: [ALL]
  • mem_limit and pids_limit
  • an image pinned tag@sha256:digest. The Hub comes from HUB_IMAGE; enroll and group-gate are built from enroll/Dockerfile / group-gate/Dockerfile, whose base images are pinned. group-gate's Python dependencies are exact pins with hashes in group-gate/requirements.txt, installed wheels-only with pip install --require-hashes

CI fails if any of these is missing.

Service User Root FS cap_add Healthcheck Notes socket-proxy-traefik / -hub root read-only (tmpfs /run) SYS_CHROOT /_ping Exception: HAProxy needs root to open the root-owned socket and chroots to / traefik root read-only (tmpfs /tmp) NET_BIND_SERVICE traefik healthcheck --ping Exception: root for ports 80/443 and the root-owned ACME volume. Without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE it reads files by mode only (certs/server.key is group 0, 0640) postgres 70:70 read-only (tmpfs /var/run/postgresql, /tmp) — pg_isready /var/lib/postgresql is postgres-owned in the image, so the entrypoint needs no chown vault 100:1000 read-only (tmpfs /tmp) — vault status disable_mlock (raft), so no IPC_LOCK. Reads secrets/vault-unseal/ via group 1000 lldap 1000 (-rootless image) read-only (tmpfs /tmp) — lldap healthcheck keycloak 1000 (image) writable (tmpfs /tmp) — /health/ready Exception: start re-augments the server into /opt/keycloak/lib because the x509 lookup provider is a build option. A custom pre-built (--optimized) image would allow read-only forward-auth (oauth2-proxy) 65532 (distroless) read-only — none Exception: the image has no shell or HTTP client group-gate 10003:10003 (USER in Dockerfile) read-only (tmpfs /tmp) — /healthz Image portcullis-group-gate: pinned python alpine base + cryptography (CRL parsing) and PyJWT (token claims) + the script. Only world-readable mounts hub 10001:10001 (image) read-only (tmpfs /tmp, /home/hub) — image HEALTHCHECK (/healthz) Writes /data (volume) and /project/templates (chowned to 10001 by ./portcullis up). Go; libraries: yaml.v3, alecthomas/participle/v2 (custom-override and rule parser), go-ldap/ldap/v3, hasura/go-graphql-client, Nerzal/gocloak/v14, moby/moby/client + api enroll 10002:10002 (USER in Dockerfile) read-only — /healthz Reads secrets/enroll/ via group 10002 prometheus, alertmanager, blackbox, textfile-exporter (profile monitoring) 65534:65534 read-only — /-/ready, /-/healthy, /metrics monitoring network is internal; nothing published. Alertmanager's only egress is the alerting network grafana (profile monitoring) 472:472 read-only (tmpfs /tmp) — /api/health Header auth only from PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP; login form and basic auth off

Throwaway containers the CLI starts:

  • the chown helper: pinned alpine, --network none, only CAP_CHOWN
  • for backups, the volume snapshot and LLDAP check: the portcullis-group-gate image (built first if missing), the volume owner's uid, --network none, read-only, no capabilities
  • restic: pinned, the operator's uid, read-only, no capabilities; --network none for a local repository
  • for backup verify, a postgres without network

items.title: Secrets the containers read
items.text:
The CLI keeps these operator-owned with the container's group, so the operator can still rewrite them and nobody else can read them. It repairs them (secrets_fix_perms) on every init, up, upgrade, vault init and restore.

Path Group Mode Read by secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key 1000 0640 (dir 0750) vault (auto-unseal) secrets/enroll/{role-id,secret-id} 10002 0640 (dir 0750) enroll secrets/enroll/{invite-client-secret,keycloak-client-secret,invite-api-secret} 10002 0640 enroll (invite IdP client, Keycloak service account portcullis-enroll, Hub invite API) secrets/hub/core.env 10001 0640 (dir 0750) Hub (as /project/.env) secrets/hub/lldap/{username,password} 10001 0640 (dir 0750) Hub (/run/portcullis/lldap, LLDAP account portcullis-hub, lldap_admin) secrets/hub/invite/secret 10001 0640 (dir 0750) Hub (/run/portcullis/invite/secret, same value as enroll's invite-api-secret) secrets/monitoring/prometheus/{vault-token,tls-targets.json} 65534 0640 (dir 0750) Prometheus (Vault metrics token: policy portcullis-metrics) secrets/monitoring/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml 65534 0640 (dir 0750) Alertmanager (receivers incl. SMTP password / webhook URLs) secrets/monitoring/grafana/admin-password 472 0640 (dir 0750) Grafana certs/server.key (dev/CI only) 0 0640 Traefik templates/ owner 10001 0755 Hub (writes)

Without root, the CLI changes owner/group through a throwaway container (pinned alpine, --network none, --cap-drop ALL --cap-add CHOWN). Anyone who can run docker is root-equivalent anyway.

The Hub never sees the core .env. It gets secrets/hub/core.env, which holds only what templates may reference: PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN, PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP, the proxy subnet and range, PORTAL_DISPLAY_NAME, HEADSCALE_*, HEADPLANE_*, NETBIRD_*, COTURN_*, and the names listed in HUB_SHARED_ENV. Core secrets are refused. ./portcullis up rewrites the file in place. secrets/ and backups/ are masked from the Hub with empty tmpfs mounts.

items.title: Header spoofing protections
items.text:
• Entrypoint. The websecure entrypoint has no forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs, so Traefik deletes client-supplied X-Forwarded-* and X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert(-Info) headers. aliasHeadersStrategy=delete also drops alias spellings such as X_Forwarded_Tls_Client_Cert. The cert headers that group-gate, enroll and Keycloak see therefore always describe a certificate Traefik verified.
  • Forward-auth headers. Traefik's forwardAuth deletes every authResponseHeaders entry from the upstream request and re-adds only the values oauth2-proxy and group-gate return. A client can't send its own X-Forwarded-User or X-Auth-Request-Groups through.
  • No stale groups from Keycloak's cache. Keycloak's LDAP federation runs with cachePolicy=NO_CACHE (realm export, enforced on existing realms by ./portcullis keycloak configure): a removed membership or changed attribute in LLDAP is in the user's next token (forward-auth refreshes every minute), not held in a cached user until eviction or the daily sync.

  • Identity is the LLDAP username, never the email. LLDAP lets users edit their own mail, including to someone else's address. So:

    • Keycloak's LDAP federation does not trust it (trustEmail=false, tokens carry email_verified=false).
    • oauth2-proxy's session user is always the token's sub (Keycloak's user UUID). Its alpha userIDClaim is only a deprecated alias of emailClaim, so it is not used (CI rejects it). Instead oauth2-proxy/alpha.yaml builds X-Auth-Request-User, X-Forwarded-User and X-Auth-Request-Preferred-Username from the preferred_username claim, keeps emailClaim: email, and accepts the unverified email (insecureAllowUnverifiedEmail) because nothing authorises by it.
    • group-gate reads the username only from X-Auth-Request-Preferred-Username (set by portcullis-auth, which must run first) and denies the request when it is missing. It never falls back to the email or sub.
    • Apps get X-Forwarded-User / X-Auth-Request-User = immutable username, and X-Forwarded-Email / X-Auth-Request-Email = email (display only).
    • Every identity header is in the forward-auth middlewares' authResponseHeaders, which is what strips client-supplied copies.
    • Apps also get X-Auth-Request-Groups. All of these headers are authResponseHeaders of the forward-auth middlewares, so Traefik deletes client-supplied copies (the e2e test sends spoofed ones). Header-auth apps must log users in by X-Forwarded-User as a username and take the email from X-Forwarded-Email.
    • enroll and the Hub use X-Forwarded-User as-is (no email → username lookup). group-gate's mTLS binding compares the cert CN with that same username and requires the token's preferred_username to match it.
    • Native-OIDC apps must key accounts on sub / preferred_username and must not link existing accounts by email (e.g. Vaultwarden SSO_SIGNUPS_MATCH_EMAIL). Apps that insist on email_verified=true need their "allow unverified email" option.
    • Apps that refuse email_verified=false but accept it absent (Vaultwarden SSO signups) get the email-unverified client scope instead of email (manifest email_verified_claim: false): the email claim without email_verified. The email is no more trusted than before. Vaultwarden still matches pending email invitations by email, so its template turns invitations off (INVITATIONS_ALLOWED=false, SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false) and gates the SSO login paths with group-gate (users_vaultwarden).

    Rule: email is never an identity or account-linking key. - Header-auth apps accept identity headers only from ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP}, through the app's proxy allow-list or a small gate in front of it. Templates CI checks this statically and with a forged request (see Header Auth Pattern). - Keycloak accepts proxy headers only from PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP on portcullis-auth, decided by the TCP peer address (--proxy-trusted-addresses). The 127.0.0.1:8080 publish for the CLI's admin API is untrusted, so it can't inject a cert. See mTLS login. - Paths. Traefik's default path handling stays on (sanitizePath, decoding of unreserved %XX). Encoded /, \, ; and %00 are allowed through because apps such as GitLab and Nextcloud use them. group-gate's path_groups matching therefore normalises the path itself and denies encoded slashes and NULs that survive one decode. path_groups checks also deny a # in the URI or an encoded one in the path.

items.title: Attribute headers
items.text:
On every request group-gate allows (/ and /authenticated, app and core subdomains alike) it also returns X-Forwarded-Attr-<Header-Name> for the signed-in user's shared custom fields, read from the Hub's user-attributes.json in hub_data (contract §4.1 / §5):

  • control characters (0x00–0x1F, 0x7F) are stripped, and values over 1 KB are dropped and logged
  • then % → %25 and , → %2C in every value (so Doe, Jane stays one value; apps percent-decode each item), and the values are joined with ,. Non-ASCII is sent as UTF-8 bytes
  • field names must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(_[a-z0-9]+)*$ (at most 31 characters) and header names ^[A-Za-z0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9]+)*$; a field with an invalid name or header name is skipped (logged), the others still get their headers
  • a missing or corrupt file (logged) means no attribute headers, never a deny. Two fields on one header (compared case-insensitively) make the file corrupt

portcullis-groups forwards them with authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr-. A headers middleware can only delete headers by exact name (and the field names are the Hub's), so client-sent X-Forwarded-Attr-* are deleted by the same regex on every forwardAuth middleware (portcullis-auth, -auth-console, -groups, -self, -public-guard): Traefik removes all request headers matching it before copying the auth server's. Public routers therefore get none, and _ aliases are dropped by the entrypoints (aliasHeadersStrategy). CI sends forged ones through the gated and public test routers.

Routers with no forwardAuth middleware (keycloak, keycloak-resources, lldap (redirect only), vault-ui, enroll-invite, and in the app overlays headscale, netbird-*, docs) do not strip client-sent X-Forwarded-Attr-*. Their backends must never trust those headers (none of them reads them).

items.title: Sessions, temporary memberships and the people directory
items.text:
• Temporary memberships.
