  • Infra and monitoring images: cached by the local composite action .github/actions/cached-images.
    • The cache key is a hash of each job's pinned image list. Refs without a digest are refused.
    • After docker load, every name set by the tarball is removed. Each ref is then re-pulled by its pinned digest (with retry and backoff), so the engine reuses a loaded image only if its content-addressed ID matches the registry's config digest.
  • enroll and group-gate images: buildx layer cache (type=gha).
  • Go: module and build cache through setup-go, with go mod verify.
  • Python: pip and Playwright browsers, cached on the pinned requirements file (group-gate/requirements.txt has --require-hashes).

The revocation check waits up to 180s, because Vault rebuilds delta CRLs at most once a minute.

items.title: Releases (release.yml)
items.text:
Runs on v* tags:

  1. preflight checks two things:
    • The tag is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and CHANGELOG.md has its ## [X.Y.Z] section.
    • The HUB_IMAGE default in docker-compose.yml is ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:A.B.C@sha256:…, where vA.B.C is a published (non-draft, non-prerelease) Hub release and the tag still resolves to that digest.
  2. ci runs the full ci.yml on the tagged commit.
  3. release builds a reproducible portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz (the checkout without .git, plus VERSION) and its .sha256. It then creates the GitHub release with the changelog section, the pinned Hub image and generated notes.

See Upgrading & Releases.

items.title: Dependabot
items.text:
.github/dependabot.yml proposes weekly, grouped updates for:

  • the compose images
  • the enroll Dockerfile and Go modules
  • the GitHub Actions
  • the e2e Python requirements

Image constants in the CLI and inline images in workflows are not covered by Dependabot. They are still checked by the pin-enforcement step.

items.title: Running the core tests locally
items.text:
python3 tests/test_group_gate.py
bash tests/test_cli.sh
bash tests/test_shell_libs.sh
(cd enroll && go test ./...)
shellcheck -S warning portcullis scripts/lib/*.sh tests/*.sh
# compose validity without Docker containers:
PORTCULLIS_ROOT=/tmp/x ./portcullis init --env-only --non-interactive --domain ci.example.org --dns-provider none

items.title: lint.yml: every push and PR, forks included
items.text:
No secrets, no core checkout, read-only token. Safe for fork pull requests, so every contributor gets this feedback:

  • python tests/validate.py: the manifest schema plus repo rules (networks, volumes, middlewares, required vars, mounts, image pinning, header trust, Dependabot coverage, .core-ref). See Manifest Reference → Validation.
  • bash tests/compose-config.sh: docker compose config for every template.
  • shellcheck of the test scripts and template scripts.
  • actionlint (pinned image).

items.title: test-apps.yml: integration tests
items.text:
Triggers: push to main, pull requests from branches of the repo, and manual workflow_dispatch (inputs pr, ref, apps). It boots core infrastructure and runs tests/apps/<app>.sh for the affected templates. The trust boundary is per job:

Job Secrets What it does gate none Resolves what to test. Fork PRs run like any other PR (core is public; no job uses a secret), with .core-ref taken from the PR's base. For a manual run with pr = <n>, it resolves the PR head commit to test changes none Verifies the commit under test. Picks the apps: changed <app>/ directories and changed tests/apps/<app>.sh. A change to tests/lib.sh, .github/ or .core-ref tests all apps. With no usable base, all apps are tested fetch-core none Checks out nothing from the PR except .core-ref, read from a trusted commit (for PR runs: the PR's base, so a PR can't point CI at another core ref). Clones the public core repo anonymously at that ref, resolves the infra image list with docker compose config --images against a throwaway .env from portcullis init --env-only (failing on an empty list), packs core as an artifact, and writes the infra image cache app-images (matrix per app, push to main only) none Never runs for PRs or manual runs. For each tested app whose test boots it, reads the image list from its compose.yml (tests/app-images.sh), pulls the pinned images and writes that app's image cache (key: hash of the list). Starts no container test (matrix per app) none Downloads core by artifact ID with digest verification. Writes no cache. Loads the cached infra and app images as untrusted: removes every name a tarball sets, then binds each image (core's and the app's) with a docker pull of its tag@sha256 pin. The pull checks the manifest against the pinned digest and reuses a loaded image only if its ID (the hash of its config, which pins every layer) is the one that manifest names; otherwise it downloads the image fresh. Boots infra like core's own CI: every secret generated by portcullis init --env-only (the workflow sets none, since the shell environment would override .env), Keycloak with its production start command, setup through the core CLI (vault init, pki setup --with-server-cert, config apply --bundle-only, keycloak configure, oidc register). Checks Traefik got its static IP and that forward-auth redirects an unauthenticated request to auth.<domain>, then runs the app's test

Every job has a read-only contents: read token. The workflow deliberately does not use pull_request_target, which would run fork code with a write token.

Fork PRs get the full integration tests automatically. A maintainer can re-run one with Actions → Test Apps → Run workflow, pr = <number>. That run tests exactly the PR's head commit, and aborts if the head moved.

.core-ref holds the core ref the templates are tested against: a tag such as v1.4.0, or main during development (today: main). Changing it re-tests every template.

items.title: docs-dispatch.yml
items.text: On push to main it sends a templates-updated repository_dispatch to this docs repo, which regenerates the App Catalog. It needs the DOCS_DISPATCH_TOKEN secret. Without it the step is skipped with a notice, and the docs pick the change up on their daily rebuild.

items.title: Test helpers (tests/lib.sh)
items.text:
Area Functions Output pass, fail, info, section, report Waiting wait_for_url URL TIMEOUT NAME, wait_for_container Keycloak keycloak_admin_token, keycloak_user_token, keycloak_enable_direct_grant, keycloak_register_client LLDAP lldap_token, lldap_graphql, lldap_create_user, lldap_create_group, lldap_add_to_group, lldap_sync_keycloak Compose compose_up APP, compose_down APP, app_container_ip APP, app_logs APP Assertions assert_http_code URL CODE, assert_redirect_to_keycloak URL, assert_redirect_contains URL STRING, assert_body_contains URL STRING, assert_container_can_reach CONTAINER URL Public exceptions public_routed_prefixes <manifest> <all\|listed> [token…] prints what the Hub's public router opens; write_public_override <app> <service> <host-arg> <tier> <out> <entry…> writes the override labels the Hub would generate (tier for every router, public router behind portcullis-public-guard@docker with static-only supporting paths, exact paths, strip middleware); pass it to compose_up with COMPOSE_OVERRIDE=<file>. write_public_policy <sub> <manifest> <mode> writes the version-3 policy entry the Hub would publish into core's hub_data volume, so core's real public guard runs (clear_public_policy empties it). assert_public_path <host> <path> [curl args] / assert_gated_path … / assert_public_refused … send HTTPS requests through Traefik on the runner (no client certificate) and check the app answers / the request is redirected to auth.<domain> / the guard answers 403. grafana.sh uses them: a listed dashboard token is public; an unlisted token, /, /api/user and /public/build/ stay gated; Grafana login cookies (also PHP-mangled spellings), Authorization, X-Access-Token and auth_token query variants are refused by the guard. It needs a core with /public-guard (.core-ref). nextcloud.sh and immich.sh check their path lists statically Header trust assert_traefik_only_trust <compose> <SETTING> checks statically that the trust setting uses ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-…} and nothing trusts every peer. assert_spoofed_identity_rejected <url> [expected] sends a forged X-Forwarded-User from the CI host (never Traefik) and expects a rejection. Required for header-auth templates

compose_up mirrors the Hub: before each compose call it exports a random value for every manifest env: entry with generate: random that isn't set yet. Templates reference those as ${VAR:?}, so a missing value fails loudly.

Every template needs a tests/apps/<app-id>.sh (validate.py checks it). A static test is the minimum; copy tests/apps/scrutiny.sh. What the tests typically verify:

Auth method Checks forward-auth Unauthenticated request redirects to Keycloak; container healthy; app endpoints respond header-auth The above, plus the Traefik-only trust setting and a rejected spoofed identity native-oidc Container reaches Keycloak's discovery endpoint; the app's SSO redirect points at Keycloak; gated login/admin paths redirect public / custom App responds without authentication; container healthy

See Adding an App for a template.

items.title: Hub CI (build.yml)
items.text:
Triggers: pushes to main, tags v*, and pull requests. Every action is pinned by commit SHA.

  • test:

    • gofmt -l . must be empty
    • go vet ./...
    • go test -race -count=1 ./...
    • go build ./cmd/hub

    The unit tests cover validation, strict route parsing, the policy-file writer (collisions, deny group, snapshots, expiring array, user-attributes.json), middleware (proxy secret, CSRF), per-app locking, reconcile/drift, the Engine API client, the LLDAP client (GraphQL + LDAP Password Modify), the Keycloak client (attribute mappers), the rule parser, and the directory service (users, groups, fields, rule evaluator, exceptions, expiries, CSV import, delegated permissions, protected accounts parity). New packages: internal/rules (rule parser and evaluator), internal/directory (users, groups, fields, permissions, import, audit). TestRealTemplates loads a sibling portcullis-templates checkout if present. TestPeopleListenerHasNoAppRoutes checks that the people listener registers no app/policy/drift/compose/Docker routes. TestProtectedAccountsParity reflects over directory.Service methods to check every user-targeting operation refuses admin and portcullis-hub. - build (after test): - Multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) with SBOM and provenance (mode=max) attestations. - Tags X.Y.Z/X.Y/X/sha-<short> for release tags and edge for main. latest is disabled. - Pushed to GHCR and signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC) by digest. Pull requests build but don't push or sign.

Verify a published image with the command in Hub → Image tags.

items.title: Running workflows locally with act
items.text:
act runs GitHub Actions workflows locally in Docker:

act -l -W .github/workflows/test-apps.yml                     # list jobs (templates repo)
act -j lint -W .github/workflows/lint.yml                      # static checks, no secrets
act -W .github/workflows/test-apps.yml                         # integration (no secrets needed)
act -W .github/workflows/ci.yml                                # core CI (core repo)

The first run downloads the runner images, which can take a few minutes.

items.title: Upgrading & Releases
items.text:
Upgrade an installation from the core checkout with:

git pull
./portcullis upgrade

upgrade is safe to re-run. Every step it performs is idempotent, and it backs up first.

items.title: What portcullis upgrade does
items.text:
1. Fills in missing secrets. It generates HUB_PROXY_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET, LLDAP_JWT_SECRET or BACKUP_PASSWORD if they are empty or missing. Nothing on disk depends on those. The database and admin passwords must already be in .env, and the command stops if one is missing.
  2. Checks the networks. It validates the portcullis-proxy and portcullis-auth settings in .env against the existing Docker networks, and stops with instructions if they differ.
  3. Backs up with portcullis backup, a consistent online backup: Vault raft snapshot, pg_dump, the LLDAP/Hub/ACME volumes, .env, certs/ and secrets/. It goes to backups/<timestamp>/. Skip this with --skip-backup.
  4. Pulls images. Core images are pinned by digest in docker-compose.yml, so the pull only changes something when the pins changed in the commit you pulled. The Hub image comes from HUB_IMAGE (see below).
  5. Re-runs the setup steps.
    • vault init: unseal, enroll AppRole and policy.
    • pki setup: rewrites the client-cert role, so a changed CLIENT_CERT_TTL applies to new certificates, and refreshes the Keycloak truststore and CRL settings. An existing CA is never replaced.
    • Rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt.
  6. Restarts the stack with docker compose up -d --build and waits for Vault, PostgreSQL, LLDAP and Keycloak to be healthy. Traefik, forward-auth and Keycloak are restarted if the CA chain or truststore changed.
  7. Re-applies the identity config. It runs keycloak configure (realm settings, X.509/CRL settings, scopes, LDAP bind) and oidc register (client secrets from .env), then recreates forward-auth so it picks up a newly generated client secret.

Check the result with ./portcullis status.

Apps enabled in the Hub are separate compose projects. upgrade does not restart them. The Hub reconciles them on start and reports anything that is not running as drift.

items.title: Backups and rollback
items.text:
The backup made by upgrade is a normal local backup (see Backups). It contains the Vault unseal key and root token, so it can decrypt the CA. Protect it like the keys themselves. upgrade does not upload it off-host: run ./portcullis backup --offsite first if you want an off-host copy of the pre-upgrade state.

To roll back, check out the previous core commit (or release) and restore the backup:

./portcullis restore --list
./portcullis restore backups/<timestamp>

restore saves the current .env, secrets/ and certs/ to backups/pre-restore-<timestamp>/ before overwriting them.

items.title: Versions and releases
items.text:
How the four repositories are versioned is defined in Integration Contracts §1:

  • Tags. Every repo uses semver tags vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change to an integration contract bumps MAJOR in every repo it affects.
  • Core images are pinned tag@sha256:digest in every compose file and profile, so a core commit fully determines which Traefik, Keycloak, Vault, LLDAP, oauth2-proxy, PostgreSQL, socket-proxy and monitoring versions run. Dependabot proposes updates weekly; CI fails on anything unpinned.
  • Templates. The Hub tracks the default branch of each template source; pull updates with Sync in the Hub. The templates CI tests against the core ref in its .core-ref.

Check what you run:

./portcullis version          # core version (VERSION file or git describe) + Hub image
./portcullis version --json

items.title: Core releases
items.text:
A core release is a vX.Y.Z tag. .github/workflows/release.yml publishes it only if all of the following holds:

  1. Tag and changelog. The tag is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and CHANGELOG.md (Keep a Changelog) has a ## [X.Y.Z] section.
  2. Pinned Hub. The HUB_IMAGE default in docker-compose.yml is a released Hub tag pinned by digest (ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:A.B.C@sha256:…). That tag must be a published, non-prerelease Hub release that still resolves to that digest.
  3. CI. The full core CI (ci.yml, called as a reusable workflow) passes on the tagged commit.

Then it publishes:

  • release notes: the changelog section, the pinned Hub image, and GitHub's generated notes
  • portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz: the checkout without .git, plus a VERSION file. The tarball is reproducible: sorted, numeric owner, commit time
  • portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.sha256

Install or upgrade from a release tarball:

sha256sum -c portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz && cd portcullis-X.Y.Z

Or check out the tag in your git checkout: git fetch --tags && git checkout vX.Y.Z.

items.title: Hub image
items.text:
HUB_IMAGE selects the Hub:

  • On core main the default is ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:edge, the latest build of the Hub's main.
  • A core release pins a released Hub tag by digest, as described above.

  • Overriding it in .env? Use a released tag and its digest, never edge in production:

    HUB_IMAGE=ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3@sha256:<digest>

Hub releases are published as X.Y.Z, X.Y, X and sha-<short>. There is no latest tag. Each image is signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC). Verify it before you pin it:

cosign verify ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/porelli/portcullis-hub/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3   # top-level Digest:

No releases yet

No repository has been tagged yet. Core main therefore runs the Hub's edge, and the templates CI tests against core main. CHANGELOG.md collects everything under [Unreleased].

items.title: Changing settings during an upgrade
items.text: You changed Run ACME_STAGING or MTLS_ENABLED ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up CLIENT_CERT_TTL ./portcullis upgrade (or ./portcullis pki setup); only new certificates are affected FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET ./portcullis oidc register && ./portcullis up An empty rotatable secret (to rotate it) ./portcullis upgrade generates a new one HUB_IMAGE ./portcullis up Network ranges See Security & Hardening → Networks. Docker can't change an existing network in place

items.title: TLS Certificates & mTLS
items.text:
Portcullis has two TLS toggles in .env. They are independent of each other:

Setting .env variable Default What it controls Certificate source ACME_STAGING false Staging (test) vs production (trusted) Let's Encrypt certs Client certificates MTLS_ENABLED true Whether Traefik requests mTLS client certs (PIV/YubiKey)

After changing either one, run:

./portcullis config apply
./portcullis up

config apply rewrites traefik/dynamic/tls.yml (Traefik hot-reloads it), sets ACME_CA_SERVER in .env, and rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt. up recreates Traefik when its environment changed.

items.title: Production (ACME_STAGING=false, the default)
items.text:
• Uses the Let's Encrypt production CA, which all browsers trust.
  • Rate limits apply: 50 certificates per registered domain per week.
  • One wildcard certificate (<domain> + *.<domain>) covers every app, so individual subdomains never appear in Certificate Transparency logs.

items.title: Staging (ACME_STAGING=true)
items.text:
• Uses the Let's Encrypt staging CA. There are no rate limits, but browsers will not trust the certificate. Use it while you iterate on DNS setup.
  • App containers that call Keycloak over HTTPS mount certs/ca-bundle.crt. config apply builds it from the system CAs, the internal Portcullis PKI chain, and the Let's Encrypt staging root (only when ACME_STAGING=true). init, up and upgrade rebuild it too.

Browser workarounds for staging certs: start Chrome with --ignore-certificate-errors, accept the risk in Firefox, or use curl -k.

items.title: Switching
items.text:
1. Set ACME_STAGING=true or false in .env.
  2. Run ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up. config apply notices the flip and clears Traefik's acme.json, so Traefik requests a new certificate.
  3. Wait about 2 minutes for the DNS-01 challenge: docker compose logs -f traefik 2>&1 | grep -i acme.

items.title: TLS tiers
items.text:
With MTLS_ENABLED=true, Traefik offers three TLS option sets (traefik/dynamic/tls.yml):

Tier Traefik option Behavior protected RequireAndVerifyClientCert Client cert required. Without one, the TLS handshake fails authaware VerifyClientCertIfGiven Client cert optional. Verified against certs/ca-chain.crt if present public NoClientCert No client cert requested

All core routers (auth, hub, enroll, traefik, directory) use authaware. For apps, the Hub derives the tier from the app's access policy and writes it into a per-app compose override. You change it by editing the policy in the Hub, not the template's compose.yml.

items.title: Issuing certificates
items.text:
Client certificates come from Vault's PKI (pki_int, role client-cert). The key is generated on the YubiKey and never leaves it.

  • Admin enrollment: at https://enroll.<domain> (requires lldap_admin), either by pasting a CSR made with ykman or through the guided flow, or on the host with ./portcullis cert enroll <user> [email].
  • What Vault signs: the role takes the CN from the caller, never from the CSR, and enroll only signs CSRs whose subject is exactly the user. The certificate has the clientAuth EKU.

items.title: Lifetime and renewal
items.text:
Certificates live CLIENT_CERT_TTL, default 720h (30 days).

Why 30 days. A very short lifetime (say 24 hours) would mean renewing with the YubiKey every day; in practice certificates expire and users fall back to weaker factors. A short lifetime would only be standing in for revocation, and Portcullis enforces revocation everywhere a certificate is accepted (see Revocation), so the lifetime just sets how often people renew. 90 days (2160h) is reasonable if you revoke lost keys promptly.

./portcullis pki setup (also run by upgrade) rewrites the Vault role with the current value. Only certificates issued afterwards are affected.

Self-service renewal at https://enroll.<domain>/self is open to any signed-in user, for their own certificate only. It runs on router enroll-self with portcullis-self@docker, which is group-gate's /authenticated check: revocation and host checks, but no lldap_admin requirement. Renewal succeeds only if all of these hold:

  • the browser presents the user's current, valid, unrevoked certificate (Traefik passes it to enroll via client-cert-pem@file)
  • its CN is the signed-in user
  • Vault issued exactly that certificate
  • the pasted CSR is for the same public key: ykman piv keys export 9a + ykman piv certificates request

An expired or revoked certificate cannot be renewed this way. An admin re-enrolls the key instead.

CLI renewal on the host, with the YubiKey attached: ./portcullis cert renew <user>.

Expiry warnings. These list users whose newest certificate has fewer than CERT_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS (default 7) days left:

  • ./portcullis status (and vault.certs_expiring in status --json)
  • ./portcullis cert list, which marks them expiring
  • the enrollment UI, which flags them

items.title: mTLS login through Keycloak
items.text:
auth.<domain> uses the authaware tier, so the browser can present the YubiKey cert to Keycloak:

  1. Traefik verifies the cert against certs/ca-chain.crt.
  2. Traefik forwards it PEM-encoded in X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert (middleware client-cert-pem@file).
  3. Keycloak reads the header with its built-in traefik x509 lookup provider (--spi-x509cert-lookup--provider=traefik). The provider understands Traefik's passTLSClientCert pem: true format.

The realm's X.509 authenticator (x509-config) then:

  • maps the Subject CN to the LLDAP username
  • re-validates the chain against certs/truststore/ (written by pki setup, mounted as Keycloak's truststore), and checks the validity period and the clientAuth EKU
  • checks the CRLs at http://vault:8200/v1/pki_int/crl and .../crl/delta (##-separated in crl-relative-path). Keycloak caches each for at most 60 s. pki_int has auto_rebuild=true (keeps the full CRL from going stale) and therefore enable_delta=true: Vault does not rebuild the full CRL on revoke. New revocations land in the delta CRL, rebuilt every minute, until the next full rebuild. ./portcullis cert revoke also rotates the full CRL immediately
  • fails closed on the CRL: if the CRL cannot be fetched, the X.509 login fails. x509-cert-auth-crl-abort-if-non-updated=true (Keycloak's actual key, with a dash) also rejects a CRL past its nextUpdate. Vault never lets it get that stale: pki setup sets pki_int/config/crl to expiry=72h auto_rebuild=true auto_rebuild_grace_period=12h

./portcullis keycloak configure pushes the x509-config settings from keycloak/realm-export.json to an existing realm.

items.title: Trusted proxy address
items.text:
A cert header carries only the public certificate, so anyone who could put one in front of Keycloak could log in as that user. Three things prevent it:

  • Keycloak only trusts the header from Traefik. Keycloak's header-based lookup providers (traefik included) return no certificate unless the request comes from a trusted proxy (HttpRequest.isProxyTrusted()). With --proxy-trusted-addresses=${PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP}, Keycloak (Quarkus) decides that from the TCP peer address of each request, and overwrites any X-Forwarded-Trusted-Proxy header the client sent (ForwardedParser, run before routing). The only trusted address is Traefik's fixed IP on the internal portcullis-auth network. That IP is outside the network's dynamic range, so no other container can get it. These sources are untrusted, so the cert header and their X-Forwarded-* are ignored:
    • requests via 127.0.0.1:8080 (the CLI's admin API access; it arrives from the Docker gateway)
    • requests from the portcullis network
    • requests from any other container attached to portcullis-auth
  • Traefik strips client-supplied cert headers. It deletes X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert* sent by the client on the entrypoint, also for requests without a TLS client cert, and drops their _/. aliases (aliasHeadersStrategy=delete).
  • CI tests it. The build-and-test job logs in through Traefik with a real cert, which must succeed. Then it sends the same cert as a forged header straight to Keycloak from the portcullis and portcullis-auth networks and from 127.0.0.1:8080, with the realm's HTTPS requirement temporarily off so only the proxy gate can stop it. None may yield an authorization code.

See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Sign-in levels (Keycloak browser flow)
items.text:
The realm's browser flow portcullis-universal (kept equal to keycloak/realm-export.json by ./portcullis keycloak configure) has no password:

acr (LoA) Satisfied by amr pwd (1) the client cert (automatic when the browser presents one) or a passkey mtls / hwk hwk (2) reaching LoA 1: every LoA 1 factor is hardware-backed, so no second touch (same) mtls (3) the client cert mtls

oauth2-proxy asks for hwk by default; group-gate asks for mtls when a policy needs the cert. Keycloak's step-up on an existing session asks only for the levels it has not reached (no prompt=login).

A user's first passkey comes from a one-time setup link (./portcullis invite <user>, or the Hub): Keycloak 26.8 cannot enrol a passkey from inside the flow (WebAuthnPasswordlessAuthenticatorFactory.isUserSetupAllowed() is false). The setup link signs the user in through the hidden identity provider portcullis-invite (enroll) with LoA 2 / amr hwk, after the passkey registration it requires. Details: Security & Hardening and Authentication Policies.

items.title: mTLS binding (group-gate)
items.text:
A token with amr=mtls proves that a cert was used at login. Sometimes an app's policy is satisfied only through the mtls factor:

  • mtls alone
  • all including mtls
  • any where mtls is the only factor present in the token

Then group-gate also requires the current request to carry a client cert that is not revoked and whose CN equals the session's preferred_username. Otherwise the user gets the step-up page (acr_values=mtls).

So a session opened with a cert that is revoked later stops working immediately. So does a session replayed from another browser without the key.

items.title: Revocation
items.text:
./portcullis cert list                # find the serial (--all includes revoked)
./portcullis cert revoke <serial>     # revoke (add --yes to skip the prompt)
./portcullis cert sync                # rewrite the serial list from Vault

Traefik does not check CRLs. A TLS handshake with a revoked but unexpired cert still succeeds. Revocation is enforced in three places:

  1. group-gate, on every request (portcullis-groups@docker and portcullis-self@docker). client-headers@file (Traefik passTLSClientCert with serialNumber: true) passes X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info to the backend and to every later forward-auth middleware. group-gate returns 403 when the cert's serial is revoked, before any other check. It has two sources:
    • The serial list certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt. cert revoke and cert sync rewrite it atomically from Vault's list of revoked serials, and group-gate re-reads it when it changes. If Vault can't be queried, the file is left unchanged and the command fails: it never "un-revokes" by writing an empty list. If the file exists but can't be read, group-gate denies every request that presents a cert (fail closed).
    • Vault's full and delta CRL (GATE_CRL_URL = http://vault:8200/v1/pki_int/crl, GATE_DELTA_CRL_URL = .../crl/delta), re-fetched every 60 s (GATE_CRL_REFRESH_SECONDS). The union is enforced. It also covers revocations made directly through the Vault API or UI: they reach the delta CRL within about 2 minutes (Vault's periodic rebuild runs once a minute) and are denied at group-gate's next refresh. If Vault is unreachable, the last good copy of each CRL is kept and the serial list still applies.
  2. Keycloak X.509 login: the CRL check above. It fails closed when the CRL is unavailable or stale.
  3. mTLS binding: sessions on mTLS-only policies need the unrevoked cert on every request.

Coverage. Revocation covers:

  • every router whose middleware chain has client-headers@file before portcullis-groups@docker (all core routers and the default templates)
  • new Keycloak X.509 logins
  • sessions on mTLS-only policies

Not covered. Routers that rely on the TLS client cert alone, e.g. a protected-tier router without portcullis-groups@docker. There the cert works until it expires. Password and WebAuthn sessions of the same user are also not affected; sign them out in the Keycloak admin console if needed.

items.title: Vault: server mode, auto-unseal and AppRole
items.text:
Vault runs in server mode with integrated (raft) storage on the vault_data volume (vault/vault.hcl, data in /vault/file), so the CA survives restarts. The listener is plain HTTP on the internal portcullis network, and on 127.0.0.1:8200 on the host only. The container runs as the image's non-root vault user (100:1000).

./portcullis vault init is idempotent and is run by init, upgrade and restore. It does three things:

  1. Init, on the first run only, with one key share, threshold 1. It writes to secrets/ (dir 0700, gitignored):
    • secrets/vault-init.json: the root token and unseal key (0600)
    • secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key: mounted read-only into the vault container. Owned by you, group 1000, 0640 (dir 0750)
  2. Unseal. After that, vault/entrypoint.sh unseals automatically on every container start: up, restart, host reboot.
  3. Least privilege for enroll. It creates the AppRole portcullis-enroll with policy vault/policies/enroll.hcl, which allows only pki_int/sign/client-cert, listing pki_int/certs and reading pki_int/cert/*. The credentials in secrets/enroll/ (group 10002 = the enroll user, 0640) are mounted read-only into enroll. Enroll logs in for 1-hour tokens and logs in again before expiry or on a 403. There is no static or root token in .env. Rotate the secret-id with ./portcullis vault rotate-enroll-secret.

The admin commands (pki setup, cert enroll|renew|revoke|list|sync, status) use the root token from secrets/vault-init.json, or VAULT_TOKEN if exported. They use the host vault CLI if it is installed, otherwise the CLI inside the vault container. The token is passed by environment-variable name, never on the command line. secrets/ and backups/ are masked from the Hub container with empty tmpfs mounts.

pki setup is idempotent and never replaces an existing CA: it only recreates missing pieces such as the client-cert role or the exported CA files. If it finds an incomplete PKI (an earlier run aborted before the intermediate was signed), it wipes and recreates it; any Vault error aborts instead of being mistaken for "no PKI". If Vault has no CA but certs/ca-chain.crt exists (Vault data lost), it refuses to create a new one. Restore a backup, or pass --force and re-enroll every certificate. See the CLI Reference.

certs/server.key is written 0640 with group 0 (Traefik runs as root but without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE). When the CLI is not run as root, it changes group ownership through a throwaway root container (pinned alpine, only CAP_CHOWN, no network).

Trade-off of auto-unseal. The unseal key lives on the same host as the encrypted data. Root on the host, or anyone who can read secrets/, can unseal Vault. What it does protect: a copy of the vault_data volume alone is useless. Several Shamir shares on the same disk would add nothing, hence one share.

For stronger guarantees, remove the secrets/vault-unseal mount and unseal by hand after each restart (docker compose exec vault vault operator unseal), or use a cloud KMS auto-unseal.

Keep an offline copy of secrets/vault-init.json. Backups made by portcullis backup and upgrade include secrets/ (and a raft snapshot of Vault), so protect them like the keys themselves. Off-host copies are encrypted with BACKUP_PASSWORD (see Backups).

items.title: Disabling mTLS (MTLS_ENABLED=false)
items.text:
All three tiers then behave like public: no client certificates are requested anywhere. Authentication is purely Keycloak passkeys (WebAuthn); there is no password sign-in. You don't need ykman or PIV setup. This is a good choice if you only want YubiKey tap-to-authenticate.

Routers that rely on mTLS alone become unauthenticated

WebAuthn only protects routers that also run forward-auth (portcullis-auth@docker). A router on the protected tier with no forward-auth middleware, such as the Vault UI template, relied on the client certificate as its authentication. With MTLS_ENABLED=false, that router becomes open: there is no WebAuthn fallback. Before you disable mTLS, add portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker to such routers, or disable them.

Also note:

  • App policies that require the mtls factor can no longer be satisfied, so users get the step-up page.
  • X.509 login in Keycloak never fires.
# .env: MTLS_ENABLED=false
./portcullis config apply
./portcullis up

items.title: Common scenarios
items.text: Scenario ACME_STAGING MTLS_ENABLED Notes First DNS/ACME experiments true false Untrusted certs, WebAuthn only Production, WebAuthn only false false Trusted certs, no certificate management Production, full mTLS false true PIV certs for browsers and CLI/API, WebAuthn fallback Development / CI true true Everything, including mTLS flows

items.title: "Your connection is not private" / NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID
items.text: You are on staging certificates. Switch to ACME_STAGING=false, or launch Chrome with --ignore-certificate-errors.

items.title: App shows "unable to get local issuer certificate"
items.text:
The app container cannot verify Keycloak's TLS cert. Check that:

  • certs/ca-bundle.crt exists (./portcullis config apply --bundle-only)
  • the container mounts it (./certs/ca-bundle.crt:<path>:ro in the template's compose.yml)
  • the runtime uses it: NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for Node.js, SSL_CERT_FILE for Go

items.title: mTLS: ERR_BAD_SSL_CLIENT_AUTH_CERT
items.text: The client certificate is invalid, expired, or not signed by the Portcullis CA. Renew it at https://enroll.<domain>/self while it is still valid; otherwise an admin re-enrolls it.

items.title: mTLS: ERR_SSL_CLIENT_AUTH_CERT_NEEDED
items.text: The router is on the protected tier and requires a client cert. Enroll a PIV cert, or change the app's access policy in the Hub.

items.title: 403 "Your client certificate has been revoked"
items.text: group-gate found the cert's serial in the revoked list or the CRL. Remove the cert from the browser/keychain and have an admin re-enroll the key.

items.title: 403 "The certificate revocation list is unavailable"
items.text: group-gate cannot read certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt and therefore denies requests that present a cert. Run ./portcullis cert sync and check the file's permissions.

items.title: X.509 login in Keycloak does nothing
items.text:
Check the Keycloak logs:

  • HTTP header "X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert" is not trusted means the request did not come from Traefik's portcullis-auth address. Check PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP and that Traefik is attached to portcullis-auth.
  • A CRL error means Vault is sealed or unreachable (./portcullis status).

items.title: DNS Configuration
items.text: Portcullis uses wildcard DNS to route all subdomains to a single server. This page covers how to set up DNS records and configure your DNS provider for automatic certificate issuance.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A domain you control (e.g., example.com)
  • DNS hosted on a supported provider (Cloudflare, Porkbun, Route53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, or any lego provider)
  • A server with a public IP running Portcullis

items.title: Option A: Wildcard DNS Record (Recommended)
items.text:
Create a single wildcard A record pointing all subdomains to your server:

*.portcullis.example.com  A  203.0.113.10

This means auth.portcullis.example.com, hub.portcullis.example.com, grafana.portcullis.example.com, and every other service subdomain all resolve to your server without creating individual records.

You also need a record for the bare subdomain:

portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10

Cloudflare proxy

If using Cloudflare, disable the orange cloud (proxy) for the wildcard record. Cloudflare's proxy interferes with mTLS client certificate verification.

items.title: Option B: Individual DNS Records
items.text:
If you prefer explicit records, create one for each service:

portcullis.example.com            A  203.0.113.10
auth.portcullis.example.com       A  203.0.113.10
directory.portcullis.example.com  A  203.0.113.10
enroll.portcullis.example.com     A  203.0.113.10
hub.portcullis.example.com        A  203.0.113.10
people.portcullis.example.com     A  203.0.113.10
traefik.portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10
metrics.portcullis.example.com    A  203.0.113.10   (monitoring profile only)

You will need to add a record each time you enable a new app.

items.title: Step 2: Create a DNS Provider API Token
items.text: Portcullis needs a DNS API token to solve ACME DNS-01 challenges for wildcard certificate issuance. Only *.portcullis.example.com appears in Certificate Transparency logs -- individual subdomain names are never leaked.

items.title: Cloudflare
items.text:
1. Go to API Tokens
  2. Click "Create Token" and use the "Edit zone DNS" template
  3. Permissions: Zone > DNS > Edit
  4. Set in .env:
DNS_PROVIDER=cloudflare
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=your-token

items.title: Porkbun
items.text:
1. Go to API Access
  2. Enable API access for your domain
  3. Create an API key and secret key
  4. Set in .env:
DNS_PROVIDER=porkbun
PORKBUN_API_KEY=pk1_...
PORKBUN_SECRET_API_KEY=sk1_...

items.title: AWS Route 53
items.text:
DNS_PROVIDER=route53
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your-key
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your-secret
AWS_HOSTED_ZONE_ID=Z1234567890

items.title: DigitalOcean
items.text:
DNS_PROVIDER=digitalocean
DO_AUTH_TOKEN=your-token

items.title: Hetzner
items.text:
DNS_PROVIDER=hetzner
HETZNER_API_KEY=your-key

items.title: Other Providers
items.text:
Traefik supports 80+ DNS providers via lego. Set DNS_PROVIDER=<lego-provider-name> and its required environment variables in .env.

Traefik is configured entirely through environment variables in the core docker-compose.yml (there is no traefik.yml). If your provider's environment variables are not already listed there, add them to the traefik service's environment section in a docker-compose.override.yml (it is part of every backup).

items.title: First-time setup
items.text:
./portcullis init asks for your domain and DNS provider (credentials are read from the environment or a hidden prompt), writes them to .env and, for the providers it knows, creates the records from Step 1 for you:

./portcullis init

items.title: Creating or checking the records later
items.text:
./portcullis dns setup           # create/update A (and AAAA) for <domain> and *.<domain>
./portcullis dns setup --check   # only compare what resolves (via 1.1.1.1) with the public IP

dns setup supports cloudflare, porkbun, digitalocean, hetzner and route53 (needs the aws CLI). For other providers it prints the records to create by hand. See the CLI Reference.

items.title: Changing the provider or credentials
items.text:
Edit .env:

ACME_EMAIL=admin@example.com
DNS_PROVIDER=porkbun
PORKBUN_API_KEY=pk1_...
PORKBUN_SECRET_API_KEY=sk1_...

Then restart the stack so Traefik picks up the new environment:

./portcullis up

Traefik requests and renews the wildcard certificate automatically.

Changing the domain

PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN is baked into the Keycloak realm (redirect URIs, hostname), LLDAP_BASE_DN, the server certificate and every enabled app's config. Pick it before init; changing it later means a new install.

items.title: Step 4: Verify
items.text:
Check that the certificate was issued:

# Check Traefik logs for ACME
docker compose logs traefik | grep -i acme

# Test with curl
curl -v https://auth.portcullis.example.com 2>&1 | grep "subject:"

You should see a Let's Encrypt certificate for *.portcullis.example.com.

items.title: How ACME DNS-01 Works
items.text:
Unlike HTTP-01 challenges (which require port 80 access for each hostname), DNS-01 proves domain ownership by creating a TXT record in your DNS zone:

  1. Traefik requests a wildcard certificate for *.portcullis.example.com
  2. Let's Encrypt responds with a challenge token
  3. Traefik uses your DNS provider's API to create a _acme-challenge.portcullis.example.com TXT record
  4. Let's Encrypt verifies the TXT record exists
  5. The wildcard certificate is issued, covering all subdomains

This is why Portcullis needs your DNS provider API token -- it creates and cleans up the challenge TXT record automatically.

items.title: One domain per installation
items.text:
A Portcullis installation serves exactly one base domain, PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN, and every app lives at <subdomain>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}. This is enforced, not just a default:

  • group-gate denies every request whose host is not exactly <label>.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}, because it looks policies and groups up by that label
  • the Hub rejects templates whose routers use any other domain (Integration Contracts §4)
  • Traefik requests one wildcard certificate (${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN} and *.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN})
  • oauth2-proxy's cookie and redirect whitelist cover .${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN} only
  • Keycloak's hostname is auth.${PORTCULLIS_DOMAIN}

To serve a second domain, run a second installation. Supporting several domains in one installation would need all of the following:

  • group-gate keyed by full host, or by a domain list
  • the Hub's host validation and policy file keyed the same way
  • a certificate and DNS records per domain
  • oauth2-proxy cookies per domain: a session cookie can't span unrelated domains, so users would sign in once per domain
  • Keycloak redirect URIs for each domain

items.title: Local Development (No Public Domain)
items.text:
For local development without a real domain or ACME:

  1. Run ./portcullis init --domain portcullis.local --dns-provider none. init already issues a self-signed *.portcullis.local server certificate from the internal PKI (certs/server.crt; ./portcullis pki setup --with-server-cert recreates it)
  2. Add entries to /etc/hosts:
127.0.0.1  portcullis.local auth.portcullis.local directory.portcullis.local enroll.portcullis.local hub.portcullis.local people.portcullis.local traefik.portcullis.local
  1. Import certs/root-ca.crt into your browser or OS trust store to avoid certificate warnings

Note

mTLS with client certificates works the same way locally. The only difference is the server certificate is self-signed instead of from Let's Encrypt.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text: Get Portcullis running from zero to a working authentication gateway with one command: ./portcullis init.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Docker with the compose plugin (v2) -- Install Docker
  • openssl, jq and curl on the host (the CLI checks for them)
  • A domain you control, with DNS hosted at a provider Traefik's ACME client (lego) supports: Cloudflare, Porkbun, Route53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, ... (see DNS Configuration)
  • A server with ports 80 and 443 reachable (VPS, home server, or local machine)
  • A YubiKey (or another FIDO2 key) for WebAuthn. ykman is only needed for PIV/mTLS certificates

items.title: Before you start: DNS
items.text:
Portcullis gets one Let's Encrypt wildcard certificate for *.<domain> with an ACME DNS-01 challenge. Without working DNS, Traefik can't get a certificate and every page shows a browser warning. Two things must be in place:

  1. The domain's DNS is hosted at a supported provider, and you have an API token that can edit its DNS records. Traefik uses the token to create the temporary _acme-challenge TXT record. The token is needed even if you create the A/AAAA records yourself. Per-provider steps (Cloudflare: "Edit zone DNS", Porkbun, Route 53, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, others) are in DNS Configuration → Step 2.
  2. Records pointing at the server: <domain> and *.<domain> (A, and AAAA if the host has IPv6) → the server's public IP. ./portcullis init creates them for the providers it knows (dns setup), or prints them for you to create by hand. See DNS Configuration → Step 1.

Check before running init (or right after, if it created the records):

dig +short portcullis.example.com
dig +short test.portcullis.example.com   # any name: answered by the wildcard

Both must return the server's public IP. If the domain has a CAA record, it must allow letsencrypt.org.

Tip

For a first try, set ACME_STAGING=true in .env (see the table below): Let's Encrypt's staging service has no rate limits, so DNS mistakes don't lock you out for an hour. Switch it off with ./portcullis config apply once everything works.

No public domain (local testing)? Use --dns-provider none and the self-signed setup in DNS Configuration → Local Development.

items.title: Step 1: Clone the core repository
items.text:
git clone git@github.com:porelli/portcullis.git
cd portcullis

That is all you need to clone. The Hub image is pulled from ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub (no build step), and the Hub clones the app templates from porelli/portcullis-templates on first start.

items.title: Step 2: Run portcullis init
items.text:
./portcullis init

It prompts for:

  • Domain: your base domain, e.g. portcullis.example.com. Apps live at <name>.<domain>
  • Email for Let's Encrypt notices (default admin@<domain>)
  • DNS provider (default cloudflare) and its API credentials, read with a hidden prompt

Unattended:

CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... ./portcullis init --non-interactive \
  --domain portcullis.example.com --dns-provider cloudflare

All options are in the CLI Reference.

items.title: What init does
items.text:
1. Writes .env (mode 0600) with every secret randomly generated: POSTGRES_PASSWORD, KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD, LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, LLDAP_JWT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET, HUB_PROXY_SECRET, and BACKUP_PASSWORD (encrypts off-host backups). Docker compose refuses to start if any of them is missing, so there are no default passwords. An existing .env is kept; only empty or missing secrets are filled in.
  2. Creates DNS records for <domain> and *.<domain> pointing at this host's public IP (dns setup; skipped with --skip-dns or --dns-provider none). The wildcard covers all app and core subdomains: auth, traefik, hub, directory, enroll, people, metrics, and each enabled app.
  3. Initialises Vault in server mode with persistent raft storage. The root token and unseal key go to secrets/ (see the warning below), and the enrollment service gets a least-privilege AppRole. Vault unseals itself on every start from then on.
  4. Starts the core stack (docker compose up -d --build) and waits for Vault, PostgreSQL, LLDAP and Keycloak to be healthy.
  5. Creates the Vault PKI: root and intermediate CA for YubiKey client certificates, Keycloak's truststore, and a self-signed wildcard server cert for local use.
  6. Configures Keycloak: imports the portcullis realm (WebAuthn, X.509, LLDAP federation, step-up flows) and registers the forward-auth OIDC client with the secret from .env.
  7. Creates config/, a separate git repo holding your .env and overrides (skip with --no-config-repo; see CLI Reference).
  8. Prints the URLs of the enrollment UI, directory, identity provider, Hub and Traefik dashboard.

Every step is idempotent: if something fails (DNS not propagated yet, a slow image pull), fix it and run ./portcullis init again.

Back up secrets/ now, offline

secrets/vault-init.json holds the Vault root token and the unseal key. Losing it together with the host means losing the CA, and every client certificate with it. Anyone who has it can unseal Vault. Keep an offline copy, and treat backups made by ./portcullis backup the same way: they contain secrets/ and .env. Store BACKUP_PASSWORD offline too: without it, off-host backups can't be restored after losing the host (see Backups).

items.title: Settings in .env worth knowing
items.text:
init writes sensible defaults. The full reference with comments is .env.example in the core repo.

Variable Default Notes ACME_STAGING false true uses Let's Encrypt staging (untrusted certs, no rate limits). Apply with ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up MTLS_ENABLED true Request YubiKey client certificates. See TLS & mTLS CLIENT_CERT_TTL 720h Client certificate lifetime (30 days) HUB_PROXY_SECRET generated Shared secret Traefik adds to every request to the Hub. The Hub refuses to start without it (at least 32 characters) HUB_IMAGE ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:edge on core main Hub image. edge is the latest build of the Hub's main; a core release pins a released tag by digest. If you override it, use a released tag with its digest, e.g. ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3@sha256:… (see Upgrading & Releases) BACKUP_PASSWORD generated restic repository password for ./portcullis backup --offsite. Keep an offline copy; never rotate it BACKUP_REPOSITORY unset restic repository for off-host backups (s3:, b2:, rest:, …). See Backups COMPOSE_PROFILES unset monitoring enables Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana at metrics.<domain>. See Monitoring HUB_SHARED_ENV empty Extra variable names the Hub may pass to templates. Core secrets are refused HUB_OVERRIDE_BIND_ROOTS /srv:/mnt:/media Host directories an app's custom compose override (Hub → Expert) may bind-mount. System paths and / are refused PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET 172.31.250.0/24 Fixed subnet of the shared portcullis-proxy network PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE 172.31.250.128/25 Dynamic addresses for app containers. Must be inside the subnet and must not contain Traefik's IP PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP 172.31.250.2 Traefik's static IP on portcullis-proxy. Header-auth apps trust identity headers only from this address PORTCULLIS_AUTH_SUBNET 172.31.251.0/28 Internal Traefik ↔ Keycloak network portcullis-auth. Must not overlap the proxy subnet PORTCULLIS_AUTH_IP_RANGE 172.31.251.8/29 Dynamic range on portcullis-auth PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP 172.31.251.2 The only address Keycloak accepts proxy headers (incl. the forwarded client cert) from HUB_PEOPLE_ADDR :8889 Hub's people listener port (set by core, not operator config). Accessible to any signed-in user at people.<domain>

Change the network ranges before init, not after

Only change the PORTCULLIS_*_SUBNET / _IP_RANGE / _TRAEFIK_IP values if they collide with a host, LAN or VPN network, and do it before the first init (./portcullis init --env-only writes .env and stops, so you can edit it). Docker cannot change an existing network. For portcullis-proxy you would have to disable the apps in the Hub, run ./portcullis down, docker network rm portcullis-proxy, ./portcullis up, and re-enable the apps. ./portcullis up detects the mismatch and prints these steps. See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Step 3: Wait for the certificate
items.text:
Traefik requests the wildcard certificate with an ACME DNS-01 challenge. This usually takes 1-3 minutes:

docker compose logs -f traefik 2>&1 | grep -i acme
./portcullis status        # overall health; exits 1 if something is down

No certificate after a few minutes? Check, in this order:

  • ./portcullis dns setup --check (are the records right and public?);
  • the provider token: it must be allowed to edit DNS records of this zone (a read-only or wrong-zone token fails the challenge);
  • the Traefik log for acme errors such as rateLimited (use ACME_STAGING=true while testing) or CAA;
  • to change the provider or token, follow DNS Configuration → Changing the provider or credentials.

items.title: Step 4: First sign-in (setup link)
items.text:
Sign-in is passkey-only: there is no password anywhere in the browser flow. ./portcullis init ends with a one-time setup link for the LLDAP admin:

  1. Open the link, click Register my key and touch your YubiKey (set or enter its PIN).
  2. You are signed in and land in the Hub. No LLDAP or Keycloak login.
  3. Every later sign-in is Sign in with Passkey and one touch.

The link works once and expires after 72 h. A new one only from the server: ./portcullis invite admin --to hub adds another key (a spare); ./portcullis invite admin --to hub --replace-keys is for a lost or stolen key (removes the old keys first). The Hub never issues links for administrators.

items.title: Step 5: Create users
items.text:
In the Hub, Users & Groups (or LLDAP at https://directory.<your-domain>, which keeps its own admin / LLDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD login):

  1. Create the user. The username is the user's identity everywhere (it can't be changed later). The email is only profile data: users can edit it themselves, so it is never used to identify or link accounts.
  2. Add the user to the groups of the apps they need, e.g. users_grafana. Members of lldap_admin can reach the core admin UIs (Hub, enrollment, directory, Traefik dashboard, Keycloak's realm console).
  3. Send the user their setup link (the Hub shows it once; on the server: ./portcullis invite <user>). It lands them on https://<your-domain>/, the portal with the apps they may use.

Keycloak reads users and groups from LLDAP through its LDAP federation.

items.title: Step 6: Enable your first app
items.text:
In the Hub:

  1. Browse the App Catalog and open an app (e.g. Grafana).
  2. Fill in any required settings (media paths, etc.).
  3. Click Enable. The Hub starts the app as its own compose project, registers its Keycloak client if it has one, and publishes its group and policy to group-gate.

The app is reachable at its subdomain. Users need the app's users_<app> group if the app enforces group access.

items.title: Step 7 (optional): YubiKey client certificates
items.text:
For mTLS (PIV certificates), an admin enrolls a user's YubiKey at https://enroll.<your-domain>, or on the host:

./portcullis cert enroll alice alice@example.com

Certificates last 30 days. Users renew their own at https://enroll.<your-domain>/self. See TLS & mTLS.

items.title: Day-to-day
items.text:
./portcullis status                # health
./portcullis up / down             # start / stop the core stack
git pull && ./portcullis upgrade   # update (backs up first)
./portcullis backup --offsite      # backup, also to restic (schedule it: backup schedule --systemd)
./portcullis version               # core version + Hub image
